cards.title: Why You Show Up
cards.why: People do not keep showing up because they were told to. Three things keep them coming back — having some say in what they do, feeling like they are getting better at it, and belonging to the people doing it. Take any one away and attendance drops, whatever the programming looks like.

parts.heading: Autonomy — having some say
parts.body: Ask who wants to own something before assigning it. Share the goal and the constraints, then leave the method to them.
items: "I'd like someone to lead the community service planning — who wants to own this, and what would you need?" rather than "Alex, you're doing community service planning."
"What do you think we should do here?" before "Here's what I think we should do."
Kills it: micromanaging a task you delegated, overriding a decision without explaining why, handing out yes/no jobs that are never real ownership.

parts.heading: Competence — getting visibly better
parts.body: Calibrate the task just above where someone currently is. Too easy and they drift; too hard and they shut down.
items: Stretch assignments for members who have mastered their current role — with the support said out loud.
Break big tasks down for new members. Small wins are what build the base.
Name specific growth in public: "I want everyone to know how that was handled this week — that was not easy, and it was excellent."

parts.heading: Relatedness — belonging to the people
parts.body: Members who feel they belong show up, contribute, and recruit. Members who do not quietly disappear.
items: Learn every member's name and one specific thing about them within three meetings.
Connect members to each other, not only to you: "Have you met — you two should talk about this."
Make the mission concrete: name the ward, the event, the people reached. Specificity beats abstraction.
Missing two consecutive meetings with no contact is a belonging signal, not an attendance one. Reach out personally within 48 hours.

steps: Pick one member who has been doing the same task for more than two months. Decide whether they are still growing.
Look at your last three chapter decisions and count how much of the input was yours versus the team's.
Transfer one decision to a member this week, and say what the constraints are rather than how to do it.
cards.where: Officer team meetings, and the recruitment conversation in the first month of the year.
cards.coach: Officers hear this as three things to add. It is usually one thing to stop. Ask which of the three they already do well, and protect that before adding another.

grounding.model: Self-Determination Theory — autonomy, competence, relatedness
grounding.citation: Deci & Ryan. Relatedness section draws on Baumeister & Leary (1995); the challenge-skill calibration draws on Csikszentmihalyi.

cards.provenance: Ported 12 Sep 2026 from officers.html — the autonomy, competence and relatedness modals, collapsed into one card.

cards.title: Not Yet
cards.why: How you explain a setback to yourself decides what you do next. Treating it as a fixed limit closes the door. Treating it as a current state with a trajectory keeps it open, and the difference often comes down to one word.

parts.heading: The word
parts.body: "I'm not good at this yet." The word yet frames a current state with an implied path. Without it, the sentence is a verdict.

parts.heading: Where it shows up in HOSA
items: Not placing at a competition — "I'm just not talented" versus "what specifically can I work on before the next one?"
When feedback stings — hearing "you're not good enough" versus hearing a specific path to better.
When someone else succeeds — feeling threatened versus getting curious about how they got there.

steps: Finish this sentence honestly: "I'm not good at ___ yet."
Write the one thing you are actively doing to build it. If nothing, that is the real finding.
cards.where: After any competition result, and in the first officer debrief of the year.
cards.coach: Do not use this to talk a member out of disappointment. Let the disappointment be real first — the reframe only works after it has been heard.

grounding.model: Mindset — Carol Dweck
grounding.citation: Dweck, Mindset: The New Psychology of Success.
grounding.caveat: Large replication studies have found growth-mindset interventions produce small average effects, smaller than the original work suggested. Present it as a useful reframe, not as a reliable performance lever.

cards.provenance: Ported 12 Sep 2026 from members.html growth-mindset modal. Neuroplasticity and longitudinal-gains claims removed as overstated; caveat added per the R/P/C rule.

cards.title: The Debrief
cards.why: Experience on its own does not teach. A competition where everyone performs and then moves on produces far less than the same competition followed by twenty structured minutes. Most of the learning from a HOSA event is in the debrief, not the event.

parts.heading: Timing
parts.body: Three windows, each doing a different job.
items: Within 24 hours — how did it feel. This has to happen while the feeling is still fresh.
Within 48 hours — what worked, what changes, what the specific next step is.
Within a week — each participant writes their own reflection down.

parts.heading: Who runs it
parts.body: The person leading facilitates rather than evaluates. Ask questions, name what you observed, and hold back recommendations until after the group has done its own analysis.

steps: Book the 48-hour slot before the event happens, not after.
Open by stating one thing you personally got wrong, before anyone else speaks.
Close with one named change, one owner, and one date.
cards.where: After SLC, after any chapter event, and after an officer team misses something.
cards.coach: The chair naming their own mistake first is the mechanism, not a nicety. Teams read whether it is safe to be honest from what the person in charge does in the first sixty seconds.

grounding.model: Psychological safety and the failure debrief
grounding.citation: Edmondson (1999), Administrative Science Quarterly. Reflection-on-experience framing after Kolb (1984); written reflection after Pennebaker (1997).
grounding.caveat: The retention comparison between written and verbal reflection that appeared in the original build has been removed — the figure could not be sourced.

cards.title: The Five Moves
cards.why: Almost everything a chapter decides can be handled with five moves. Learn those five, use them on one real decision at every meeting, and you can function in any deliberative body — including the ILC Business Session — without ever memorising the rest of the book.

parts.heading: The five, in order
items: Move it — “I move that…” One sentence, stated as the thing you want the chapter to do.
Second it — a second means one other person thinks it is worth discussing. It is not agreement.
Debate it — the chair recognises speakers; each speaker addresses the chair; nobody speaks twice until everyone who wants to has spoken once.
Amend it — insert words, strike words, or strike and insert. An amendment is voted on before the motion it changes.
Vote it — a voice vote first. If the result is in doubt, anyone may call for a division, which is a show of hands or standing count.

parts.heading: What each move is for
parts.body: The test asks purpose, not vocabulary. A move you can name but cannot place is not yet learned.
items: A motion exists so the chapter debates one clear proposal rather than a topic.
A second exists so one person cannot consume the meeting alone.
Debate rules exist so the quietest member gets a turn before the loudest gets a second one.
Amendment exists so a nearly-right proposal gets fixed instead of killed.
Division exists so a close vote is counted rather than guessed.

steps: At the next chapter meeting, take one decision the chapter genuinely needs to make and run it using only these five moves. Not a simulation — a real decision.
Print the card. Keep it at the officer table for the first three meetings, then take it away.
Once a month, ask a member at random to name the five moves in order. Spacing, not review, is what makes it stick.
cards.where: Every chapter business meeting. You will already be ready for the Parliamentary Procedure band of Organizational Leadership, and for the floor at ILC.
cards.coach: The instinct is to teach the whole procedure in September. Do not. Five moves, retrieved monthly on real business, outperforms one comprehensive workshop that nobody retains by October. If a member asks about a motion not on this card, that is the signal to move them to Lead a Team, not to expand this card.

grounding.model: Robert’s Rules of Order Newly Revised, 12th edition; RONR In Brief, 3rd edition
grounding.citation: RONR 12th ed. (effective 1 September 2020; a revised printing issued June 2026 is the same edition). The tiered, spaced-retrieval design follows Dunlosky et al. (2013), Psychological Science in the Public Interest — practice testing and distributed practice rated high utility; massed single-session instruction rated low.

cards.title: Quorum and the Order of Business
cards.why: Two things decide whether a meeting can act at all and what it does first. A chapter that skips them makes decisions that can be challenged later, and wastes the first twenty minutes every time.

parts.heading: Quorum
parts.body: The minimum number of members who must be present for the chapter to conduct business. It is set in the chapter’s bylaws — if yours do not say, the default under RONR is a majority of members. Without quorum a meeting can hear reports and set a next date; it cannot decide anything.
items: The chair confirms quorum at the start, out loud, and the secretary records it.
If members leave and quorum is lost, business stops. Anything decided after that point can be challenged.
Know your number. If your chapter has never checked its bylaws for this, that is the first action.

parts.heading: The standard order of business
parts.body: RONR’s default sequence. A chapter may adopt its own, but this is what an unfamiliar chair should reach for.
items: Reading and approval of minutes
Reports of officers, boards and standing committees
Reports of special committees
Special orders — business previously scheduled for this meeting
Unfinished business and general orders — anything carried over
New business

steps: Find the quorum number in your chapter bylaws. If there is no bylaws document, that is a Lead Beyond problem — flag it to your advisor now.
Put the six-line order of business at the top of the next agenda, verbatim.
Have the chair state quorum before the first item, every meeting, until it is a habit.
cards.where: The first two minutes of every meeting. Also a direct test item in the Organizational Leadership parliamentary band.
cards.coach: Chapters that ‘never seem to get through the agenda’ almost always lack an order of business, not time. Ask to see the last three agendas before offering any other advice.

grounding.model: RONR In Brief, 3rd edition — quorum; standard order of business
grounding.citation: Robert’s Rules of Order Newly Revised In Brief, 3rd ed.; RONR 12th ed. §3 (quorum), §41 (order of business).

cards.title: Who Governs What
cards.why: ‘HOSA says’ is not a sentence. There are four levels, each decides different things, and most of the confusion in a chapter — who to ask, who can change a rule, why a deadline in DC differs from the one on hosa.org — comes from not holding the map. This card is the map.

parts.heading: The four levels
items: HOSA Inc. — the corporate entity. A Board of Directors and a Headquarters staff. Sets the competitive event guidelines, the Bylaws, affiliation, and ILC. Not a student body.
International Executive Council — the elected student officers of International HOSA. Represent members, run the ILC business session, do not set policy on their own.

Chartered Association — DC HOSA. The State Advisor, state staff, and the State Executive Council. Runs the state calendar, SLC, cut scores, the DC internal ILC deadline, and any DC divergence from the international model.
Local Chapter — your school. The chapter advisor, chapter officers, and members. Decides its own meetings, projects, events entered, and whether it affiliates.

parts.heading: What each cannot decide
parts.body: The part that prevents most mistakes.
items: A Local Chapter cannot change a competitive event rule or a state deadline. Ask; do not assume.
The State Executive Council cannot change the DC HOSA Bylaws or Standing Rules on its own — those change by the process written into them.
The International Executive Council does not write the event guidelines. HOSA Inc. does.

DC HOSA can set an earlier deadline than International HOSA, and does — the DC internal ILC deadline is earlier than the international one so the State Advisor can review every submission while problems are still fixable.

parts.heading: The words
parts.body: Precision here is not pedantry; it is how you know which level you are talking to.
items: International HOSA, never “national HOSA” or “nationals”.
ILC — International Leadership Conference. There is no NLC.
Chartered Association, not “state chapter”. Local Chapter, not “club”.
State Executive Council or SEC, not “state board”.

steps: Take the last three questions your chapter sent up the chain. For each, name the level that actually decides it.
Put the four-level map on the wall at your next officer meeting and leave it there.
Before the next “can we…” question leaves the chapter, check which level owns it.
cards.where: Every time a question leaves the chapter. It is also the HOSA Inc. and Organizational Structure bands of Organizational Leadership together — 28% of that test.
cards.coach: When an officer uses “nationals” or “HOSA said”, do not correct the word — ask which of the four levels they mean. The word fixes itself once the map is held.

grounding.model: HOSA organisational structure — HOSA Handbook Sections A–C; HOSA Bylaws
grounding.citation: HOSA Handbook Sections A, B and C; HOSA Bylaws (current edition at hosa.org). DC divergences per DC-FACTS.md. Structure drawn from the hosa.org website is volatile — date anything taken from it.
grounding.caveat: Specific office names and board composition change. Verify against hosa.org before each affiliation year rather than trusting this card’s wording.

cards.title: Chair a Meeting That Ends on Time
cards.why: Most chapter meetings are not too long because there is too much to do. They are too long because the agenda is a list of nouns, nobody knows what a decision looks like, and the first two minutes were lost. All three are fixable before the meeting starts.

parts.heading: Agenda as questions
parts.body: Rewrite every agenda line from a topic into the question the chapter has to answer.
items: “Fundraiser” becomes “Do we commit to a February fundraiser, and who leads it?”
“SLC” becomes “Which events are we entering, and by when do we need names?”
If a line cannot be turned into a question, it is an announcement. It goes in an email, not on the agenda. This one conversion removes about a third of most chapter agendas.

parts.heading: The first two minutes
parts.body: How the chair opens sets the whole meeting. Research on workplace meetings finds the chair’s opening behaviour has a disproportionate effect on what follows.
items: Start at the stated time, even if the room is half full. The people who are on time are the ones you are rewarding.
State quorum, state the end time, state what the meeting must decide today.
Say one specific thing that went well since the last meeting, with a name attached.

parts.heading: The parking lot
parts.body: A visible list for things raised that are not today’s question. Revisited before adjournment, never silently dropped.
items: Write it where everyone can see it, not in the chair’s notes.
In the last three minutes, read it aloud and assign each item to a date or a person.
An item parked three meetings running is a decision the chapter is avoiding. Name that.

steps: Take your next agenda and rewrite every line as a question. Delete the ones that cannot be.
Write the opening — quorum, end time, the decisions — on the top of the page and read it.
Put a parking lot on the whiteboard before anyone arrives.
cards.where: Every chapter meeting you chair. The written script is also what a chair uses in the Parliamentary Procedure team event.
cards.coach: Watch the opening, not the middle. If a chair drifts into the first item without stating quorum, end time and today’s decisions, the meeting is already lost and no amount of agenda discipline recovers it.

grounding.model: Meeting science — Rogelberg
grounding.citation: Rogelberg, The Surprising Science of Meetings (2019) and the underlying organisational-psychology research programme. Most of it was conducted on adult workplace meetings; label it as such.
grounding.caveat: Evidence base is adult workplace meetings, not student organisations. The mechanisms transfer; the effect sizes may not.

cards.title: One Motion a Month
cards.why: Officers need more than the Five Moves, but they do not need all of it in September. One new motion class each month, used on real business that month, and by February the officer team can run any meeting the chapter will ever hold.

parts.heading: The drip
parts.body: Each month adds one thing and uses it on one real item. An advisor can drop this into a chapter calendar unmodified.
items: September — the order of business; the chair’s written script; the quorum call. An officer chairs from the script.
October — Amend (including amending an amendment); Refer to committee. Refer one real decision to a committee.
November — Postpone to a certain time; Previous Question, which closes debate. Close debate properly on one item.
December — Minutes to RONR standard; the treasurer’s report. The secretary drafts minutes in competition format.
January — Precedence: why motions rank, and how to read the ladder. The chair handles a motion made out of order.
February — Committee reports, and the difference between a report and a recommendation. A committee reports and moves adoption.

parts.heading: What each motion is for
parts.body: The Organizational Leadership test asks purpose. So does real life.
items: Amend — the proposal is nearly right. Fix it rather than kill it.
Refer to committee — the chapter does not have enough information to decide today. Send it to people who will get the information.
Postpone to a certain time — the chapter has the information but not the right people or moment. Name the meeting it comes back to.
Previous Question — everyone has been heard and the debate is now repeating. Requires two-thirds, because ending debate early is a serious thing to do to a minority.
Postpone Indefinitely — dispose of a motion the chapter does not want to vote on directly. The polite kill.

parts.heading: The cold-call
parts.body: At the top of each officer meeting, four questions on the material from two months ago. Not last month. Two months. That gap is the intervention.

steps: Print the six-month table and put it in the chapter calendar today.
Assign one officer to chair each month’s meeting from the script — rotate, so nobody hides behind the president.
Start the cold-call in November. Four questions, October material. Keep it under three minutes.
cards.where: Officer meetings, September to February. By March the secretary’s December minutes are already a Parliamentary Procedure competition asset.
cards.coach: The temptation is to skip ahead when a keen officer asks. Resist it — the schedule is the point. If they want more, point them at Precedence in Lead Beyond and let them read ahead on their own time.

grounding.model: RONR 12th ed. subsidiary motions; spaced retrieval
grounding.citation: RONR 12th ed. §§10–17 (subsidiary motions); Dunlosky et al. (2013) on distributed practice and practice testing.

cards.title: Minutes, and the Decision Log
cards.why: Minutes and a decision log are two different documents that chapters keep trying to make into one. Minutes are the governance record — formal, RONR-shaped, and what the Parliamentary Procedure event asks you to produce. The decision log is working memory. Combining them produces minutes nobody reads and decisions nobody can find.

parts.heading: Minutes — what goes in
parts.body: RONR minutes record what was done, not what was said.
items: Kind of meeting, name of the body, date, time, place; whether the chair and secretary were present; whether the previous minutes were approved.
Every main motion, exactly as adopted or as it stood when disposed of, with the name of the mover and the result.
Points of order and appeals, with the chair’s ruling.
Not: who said what in debate, the secretary’s opinion, or a summary of the discussion.

parts.heading: The decision log — one line each
parts.body: Lives beside the minutes. Date, decision, who decided, why, and the date it should be revisited.
items: “14 Oct — February fundraiser is a bake sale, not a fun run. Officer team. Fun run needs a permit we cannot get by then. Revisit 1 Dec.”
Anyone can search it. Nobody has to read a whole meeting’s minutes to find out why the chapter stopped doing something in 2024.
The revisit date is what makes it a log rather than a list. A decision with no revisit date is a decision the chapter will relitigate.

steps: Split your current record into two files today, if it is one.
For the next meeting, have the secretary produce minutes in the RONR format on the printed template.
Start the decision log with the last five decisions you can remember. Add revisit dates.
cards.where: Every meeting. The December minutes from One Motion a Month are the same document the Parliamentary Procedure team brings to the prep room.
cards.coach: Ask to see the decision log before asking about the chapter’s problems. A chapter with no log will describe the same three arguments every year and call them new.

grounding.model: RONR 12th ed. — minutes; decision records as organisational memory
grounding.citation: RONR 12th ed. §48 (minutes and reports of officers). The separate decision-log practice is a practitioner convention; label it as such.

cards.title: Virtual Meetings That Do Not Exhaust People
cards.why: Video-call fatigue is not a character flaw and it is not solved by telling people to focus. It has four identified causes, and every one of them has a mechanical fix in the meeting settings. This is rare among wellbeing topics — the advice is technical rather than exhortative.

parts.heading: Four causes, four fixes
items: Excessive close-up eye contact → use speaker view rather than gallery for groups over eight, and let people sit back from the camera.
The load of watching yourself constantly → hide self-view. This one setting does more than any other.
Reduced mobility → forty-five minute cap with a hard stop; audio-only segments for discussion-heavy blocks so people can move.
Constantly performing attentiveness → the chair asks questions by name, so members are not signalling engagement to the whole grid at once.

parts.heading: The six-line norms card
parts.body: Post it once. Enforce it by the chair’s behaviour, not by announcement.
items: Self-view hidden.
Speaker view for groups above eight.
Forty-five minutes, hard stop.
Camera-optional windows named in the agenda, not granted ad hoc.
Audio-only for discussion blocks.
Chair calls on people by name.

steps: Change your own settings first — self-view off, speaker view on.
Put the end time in the meeting title.
Mark the camera-optional segment on the agenda before sending it.
cards.where: Any virtual chapter or SEC meeting. Particularly the affiliate-wide calls where people are attending from home after school.
cards.coach: If a virtual meeting is flagging, do not add an icebreaker. Check whether the four settings are in place. They almost never are.

grounding.model: Four mechanisms of videoconference fatigue — Bailenson
grounding.citation: Bailenson (2021), Technology, Mind, and Behavior — theoretically derived, followed by the validated Zoom Exhaustion and Fatigue (ZEF) Scale.

cards.title: The Backwards-Planned Year
cards.why: A chapter calendar built forward from September is a list of hopes. One built backward from the dates that are fixed — the testing window, the registration deadline, the conference — is a set of derived deadlines nobody had to argue about. The year has two peaks in DC, not one, and a chapter that plans for March has already missed the first.

parts.heading: Fix the anchors first
parts.body: Take every date from the current DC HOSA Calendar of Events and the state deadlines. Confirm them annually — they move. The 2026–27 shape:
items: Round One testing runs in a window in late January to early February, not at the conference. This is the first peak.
Competitive event registration closes in mid-January. Count back from there to when you need names.
Round Two runs at pre-SLC offsite locations and on SLC Day 1. Offsite rounds are separate trips on separate dates.
The DC internal ILC deadline is earlier than the international one, for both registration and uploads.
Voting delegates logged by mid-November; the Standards of Excellence deadline at the end of June.

parts.heading: Derive everything else
parts.body: From each anchor, count back.
items: Event selection → two weeks before registration closes, so there is time to fix a mismatch.
Practice runway → at least eight weeks before the testing window opens. That means a December start, not a January one.
Recruitment push → before affiliation, because affiliation numbers set what the chapter can enter.
Fundraising → autumn, and hold the reserve for the one genuinely large cost, which is ILC travel. Raise in autumn, allocate in March.
Every chapter event → four weeks out, one week out, day of, forty-eight hours after. The four-phase checklist lives on the printed sheet.

steps: Get this year’s DC HOSA Calendar of Events. Write the anchors on the printed sheet, with the source and date.
Derive the chapter deadlines by counting back. Do not choose any date; derive it.
Put the derived calendar and the One Motion a Month drip on the same page. They are the same year.
cards.where: The first officer meeting of the year, and again in January when the second peak is visible.
cards.coach: Ask which dates on the chapter calendar were derived and which were chosen. Chosen dates are the ones that slip. If the advisor cannot name the DC testing window from memory, start there — it is the anchor everything else hangs on.

grounding.model: Backward design; DC HOSA competition calendar
grounding.citation: Backward planning as a practitioner convention. Every date must come from the current DC HOSA Calendar of Events and DC-FACTS.md §1 and §12 — this card gives the shape, never the dates.
grounding.caveat: Dates change every year and were amended mid-year in 2026–27. Nothing on this card is a date; it is a method for deriving them.

cards.title: Precedence — Why Motions Rank
cards.why: When two motions are on the floor at once, one of them has to be handled first. The ranking is not arbitrary — each motion outranks the one below it because it asks a more urgent question. Read the ladder as a set of reasons and it becomes memorable; read it as a list and it never will be.

parts.heading: The ladder, top to bottom
parts.body: Higher outranks lower. A motion can be made while a lower one is pending; not while a higher one is.
items: Privileged motions — about the assembly itself, not the business: fix the time to adjourn, adjourn, recess, question of privilege, call for the orders of the day.
Subsidiary motions — about the main motion: lay on the table, previous question, limit or extend debate, postpone to a certain time, refer to committee, amend, postpone indefinitely.
The main motion — the actual proposal. Lowest, because everything else exists to handle it.

parts.heading: Why the order is what it is
items: Adjourn outranks everything because a body that has to leave cannot keep debating.
Previous Question outranks Amend because ‘stop talking and vote’ is a more urgent question than ‘change a word’.
Postpone Indefinitely is the lowest subsidiary because it is the least urgent thing you can do to a motion — decline to decide it.
Incidental motions — point of order, appeal, division, parliamentary inquiry — have no rank. They arise from whatever is happening and are decided immediately.

parts.heading: Reading a real situation
parts.body: A main motion is pending. Someone moves to amend. Someone else moves the previous question. Amend is pending; previous question outranks it, so it is in order and is voted first. If it passes, debate ends on the amendment and the chapter votes the amendment, then the main motion.

steps: Draw the ladder from memory, then check it against the card.
At the next meeting where an amendment is pending, deliberately move the previous question and walk the room through what happens next.
Keep a running list of motions made out of order and what the chair should have said.
cards.where: January of One Motion a Month, and the Parliamentary Procedure team event, where the full ladder is tested.
cards.coach: Nobody learns precedence from the table. They learn it from the first time a motion is ruled out of order and the chair can say why. Manufacture that moment on purpose.

grounding.model: RONR 12th ed. — order of precedence of motions
grounding.citation: RONR 12th ed. §5 and the chart of motions; RONR In Brief 3rd ed.

cards.title: Bylaws and Standing Rules
cards.why: Two documents govern DC HOSA, and they change by different processes. Knowing which one a rule lives in tells you how hard it is to change and who can do it. Officers who do not know this try to fix a bylaw problem with a motion, or wait a year to fix a standing-rule problem that could have been fixed at the next meeting.

parts.heading: The difference
items: Bylaws — the constitution of the affiliate. Who is a member, what the officers are, how they are elected, how the bylaws themselves change. Amending them requires prior notice and a supermajority, and the process is written into the bylaws.

Standing rules — the operating details. Deadlines, forms, the calendar, recognition programme details. Can be adopted or amended by a majority at a meeting where they are in order, without prior notice unless the standing rules say otherwise.
Where a standing rule contradicts a bylaw, the bylaw wins. Where practice contradicts a standing rule, the standing rule is what needs amending — practice is not a rule.

parts.heading: The DC situation
parts.body: DC HOSA runs several things differently from the international model and from its own Standing Rules as currently written — competition delivery, the ILC internal deadline, several calendar dates, the Standards of Excellence deadline. Those divergences are settled decisions within the State Advisor’s authority, and they are on the list to be written into the Standing Rules. Until they are, an officer reading only the Standing Rules will be wrong about the calendar.
items: Read the current Calendar of Events alongside the Standing Rules, not instead of them.
If a rule and the calendar disagree, ask the State Advisor which is current. Do not pick.
When you find one, log it — that list is how the amendment gets written.

steps: Read the DC HOSA Bylaws and Standing Rules once, start to finish. It takes under an hour.
List every place where what the affiliate actually does differs from what the Standing Rules say.
Bring the list to the State Advisor. That is a contribution, not a complaint.
cards.where: State Executive Council orientation. Any time an officer proposes changing ‘how we do things’.
cards.coach: An SEC that has read the governing documents asks better questions all year. Assign the reading in the first month and check it was done — it is the highest-return hour in the officer calendar.

grounding.model: RONR — bylaws and rules of order; DC HOSA Bylaws and Standing Rules
grounding.citation: RONR 12th ed. §2 (rules of an assembly) and §56–57 (bylaws; amending). DC HOSA Bylaws and Standing Rules v2.2; divergences per DC-FACTS.md §12 and OPEN-ITEMS.md.
grounding.caveat: The Standing Rules amendment for the DC divergences is outstanding. This card describes the situation as of September 2026; check whether the amendment has been adopted.

cards.title: The Voting Delegate
cards.why: A voting delegate represents the Chartered Association at the ILC business session — electing the International Executive Council and voting on anything put to the assembly. It is the most direct governance role a member can hold, and the preparation is specific, dated, and mostly done before arriving.

parts.heading: How delegates are chosen and how many
items: Selection is at Chartered Association level — the State Advisor’s discretion, or as set out in the DC HOSA Bylaws or Policies and Procedures. DC HOSA has not yet written a selection method into its Standing Rules; until it does, the method is the State Advisor’s call each year.

The number is set by the division membership formula in Article V, Section 2 of the HOSA Bylaws — it steps up with membership. Confirm the current formula against the Bylaws at hosa.org each year rather than trusting a remembered figure.
Delegates are logged with International HOSA by a mid-November deadline in DC. Late is not eligible.

parts.heading: Sixty days out
parts.body: The State Advisor receives the Voting Delegate Packet from HOSA Headquarters about sixty days before ILC.
items: Read the packet, all of it.
Read every International Executive Council candidate’s resume and watch their videos on hosa.org.
Complete the Candidate Evaluation Rubric before the conference, so you meet candidates with criteria already written.

parts.heading: At ILC
parts.body: Five things, in order.
items: Voting Delegate Orientation.
Meet the Candidates Breakfast.
Chartered Association Caucus — optional, and this is where the delegation decides whether it votes as a block.
Business Session — the vote.
Recognition Session — ribbon, certificate and pin.

parts.heading: After
parts.body: Report back to the Chartered Association on how the delegation voted and why. A delegate who does not report has not finished the job.

steps: Confirm with the State Advisor how DC selects its delegates this year and by what date.
Put the three dated triggers in your calendar the day you are named.
Draft the report-back before you leave the conference, while the reasoning is fresh.
cards.where: ILC. Also the largest band of Organizational Leadership — 24% of the test is this role.
cards.coach: The delegate role is the cheapest real governance experience the affiliate has and most chapters treat it as a perk. Make it an application, with the rubric as part of it.

grounding.model: HOSA Voting Delegate process — HOSA Bylaws Article V; Organizational Leadership guideline 2026–27
grounding.citation: Organizational Leadership ILC Guidelines, September 2026 (2026–27), hosa.org; HOSA Bylaws Article V, Section 2; HOSA Handbook Section B.
grounding.caveat: The delegate-count formula and packet timing are as published in the 2026–27 guideline. Re-pull before SLC and before ILC; HOSA revises guideline files mid-season.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from OrgLeadership CE Module OL-1.

cards.title: Evaluate a Candidate
cards.why: Every election is decided either against criteria written beforehand or against charisma in the moment. Writing four or five criteria before meeting anyone is the whole skill, and it transfers directly — to chapter elections, to choosing a committee chair, to hiring later in life.

parts.heading: Write the criteria first
parts.body: Before reading a single resume. Four or five, no more.
items: What has this person actually run — not joined, run — and what happened?
Can they say what the office is accountable for, in their own words, without reading it?
Do their stated plans fit what the office can decide, or are they promising things the office cannot deliver? (See Who Governs What.)
How do they talk about the people they have led? Credit given, or credit taken?
Optional fifth, chosen by the delegation: the one thing DC HOSA specifically needs from this office this year.

parts.heading: Then apply them, in writing
parts.body: One row per candidate, one column per criterion, a mark and a line of evidence in each cell. The evidence line is what stops the mark from being a feeling.
items: Score from the resume and video before the Meet the Candidates Breakfast.
Adjust after meeting them, and write down what changed your mind. If nothing did, the criteria worked.
A delegation that shares a rubric can caucus in ten minutes instead of an hour.

parts.heading: Representative, not individual
parts.body: A delegate votes for the Chartered Association, not for themselves. The rubric is what makes that real — it is the delegation’s judgement written down, applied by one person at the ballot.

steps: Write your four criteria now, on the printed rubric, before opening hosa.org.
Score every candidate from the published materials.
Bring the completed rubric to the caucus.
cards.where: ILC elections. Chapter officer elections in spring. Any time the chapter is choosing a person for a role.
cards.coach: Ask a delegate to show you their criteria before they show you their preferred candidate. If the criteria arrive second, they were written to justify the choice.

grounding.model: Structured evaluation against pre-specified criteria
grounding.citation: Practitioner convention, consistent with the structured-interview and decision-hygiene literature; the specific rubric is a DC HOSA construction. Pairs with the Representation Boundaries card at Voice · Lead Beyond.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from OrgLeadership CE Module OL-1.

cards.title: Office Duties, Three Levels
cards.why: A chapter secretary and an International HOSA officer hold offices with the same name and overlapping duties three levels apart. Seeing them side by side does two things: it makes each office’s accountability concrete, and it shows a first-year officer that the ladder they are on goes all the way up.

parts.heading: Local Chapter
parts.body: The standard officer set from HOSA Handbook Section C. Chapters may vary it in their bylaws.
items: President — chairs meetings, holds the calendar, is the chapter’s face to the school and the affiliate.
Vice President — programme and committees; chairs in the president’s absence.
Secretary — minutes to RONR standard, the decision log, correspondence, the roster.
Treasurer — the budget one-pager, dues, the reserve for ILC, the report at every business meeting.
Reporter or Historian — the chapter’s record and its public voice.
Parliamentarian — advises the chair on procedure; the Precedence card is this office’s job.

parts.heading: DC HOSA State Executive Council
parts.body: The 2026–27 positions. Titles are set in the DC HOSA Bylaws.
items: President — chairs the SEC, represents the affiliate, holds the portfolio charters together.
President-Elect — succession; shadows the President and takes the office the following year.
Vice President of Membership — chapter growth, retention, the affiliation push.
Vice President of Community Outreach — partners, service, the community-facing calendar.
Vice President of Public Relations — affiliate communications, the newsletter, the health literacy column.
Vice President of Middle School Development — the MS division and its pipeline into secondary chapters.

parts.heading: International Executive Council
parts.body: Elected at ILC by the voting delegates. The exact set of offices and regional structure is published at hosa.org and should be confirmed there each year rather than copied from this card.
items: President and President-Elect — the same succession pattern as DC.
Vice Presidents by region and by division — representation of Chartered Associations and of the postsecondary/collegiate membership.
What they do: represent members, run the ILC business session, serve on committees. What they do not do: write the competitive event guidelines or the Bylaws.

steps: Find your office in the first column. Read the same office two columns over.
Write, in one sentence each, what your office is accountable for at your level and what the office above you is accountable for at theirs.
Bring that to your Portfolio Charter or your Transition Packet.
cards.where: Officer orientation at chapter and state level. It is also the Executive Council band of Organizational Leadership.
cards.coach: The recruitment argument is sitting in this table. A chapter secretary who can see that the same office exists at ILC is a chapter secretary who might run for it. Point at it.

grounding.model: HOSA officer structure — Handbook Section C; DC HOSA Bylaws; hosa.org
grounding.citation: HOSA Handbook Section C (chapter management); DC HOSA Bylaws v2.2 (SEC offices); International Executive Council structure at hosa.org.
grounding.caveat: International Executive Council office titles and regional structure change. The IEC column deliberately describes the pattern rather than listing current titles — verify at hosa.org each affiliation year and update the card.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from OrgLeadership CE Module OL-6. Positions only, no names, per the settled rule.

cards.title: Double-Loop Learning
cards.why: A problem can be fixed twice. Once by fixing the instance — a chapter missed a deadline, so extend it. And once by asking why this kind of problem keeps appearing and changing the thing that produces it. State-level roles are the only ones that see the pattern across every chapter, and that view is wasted if every recurrence gets the first kind of fix.

parts.heading: Single loop
parts.body: Detect the error, fix it, carry on under the same assumptions. Fast, often necessary, and it guarantees the same problem in a different form next term.
items: A chapter misses the registration deadline → the deadline is extended for them. Solved, this once.

parts.heading: Double loop
parts.body: Detect the error and examine the assumption that produced it. Slower, and it removes the category.
items: A chapter misses the registration deadline → ask why chapters keep missing this particular deadline. The form is confusing, or the date collides with a predictable school event. Fix the form or move the date. Solved, for everyone, permanently.

parts.heading: The trigger
parts.body: The third time the same type of issue arrives from a different chapter, stop fixing instances. That is the signal. Log every issue resolved; the log is what makes the third time visible.

steps: Start the pattern log — date, chapter, issue type, instance count. One line per resolved issue.
When any issue type reaches three, write one sentence stating the assumption behind the system that produced it.
Change the system once. Then watch the log for whether the category stops.
cards.where: State staff and SEC work across chapters. Any role that hears the same complaint from more than one place.
cards.coach: Most people in a support role measure themselves by how fast they resolve things. This card asks them to measure how many things they made impossible to recur. Those are different numbers and the second is the one that matters.

grounding.model: Single-loop and double-loop learning — Argyris & Schön
grounding.citation: Argyris & Schön (1978), Organizational Learning: A Theory of Action Perspective.

cards.provenance: Ported 12 Sep 2026 from state-staff.html — the double-loop section and the Pattern Log worksheet. Rehomed here per the salvage audit map-gap decision.

cards.title: Early Adopters First
cards.why: A statewide initiative launched to every chapter at once with equal effort wastes attention on chapters that are not ready and under-supports the ones that are. Adoption follows a curve, and the curve is a plan: launch with the few who will move fast, make their success visible, and let that do the persuading.

parts.heading: Find the two or three
items: Chapters with a strong advisor–SEC relationship — they respond and they trust the ask.
Chapters with a proactive officer team that has adopted a previous initiative quickly.
Not the biggest chapters. The readiest ones.

parts.heading: The sequence
items: Week one — the early adopters get the ask, concentrated support, and a named SEC contact.
Weeks two to three — their early result is made visible to everyone else. Specifically: ‘this chapter is already doing it, and here is what happened’.
Then the wider rollout, which now carries social proof. The remaining chapters adopt faster because someone else has taken the risk.
Ongoing — recognition for every chapter that engages, in public and by name of chapter.

parts.heading: Sort the rest by relationship, not by size
parts.body: Before any affiliate-wide message, sort chapters into strong, developing, and strained relationships. A blanket email works for the first and fails for the other two — those need a call, and sometimes they need state staff to bridge before an SEC ask will land.

steps: Name your two or three early adopters for the next initiative and write down why each one.
Write the week-two visibility message before you launch, so you know what success has to look like.
Sort every other chapter into the three relationship tiers on the tracker.
cards.where: Any SEC or state-staff initiative that has to move more than a few chapters. Spark One recruitment, a service campaign, a new event push.
cards.coach: When an initiative stalls, the SEC’s instinct is to send a louder message to everyone. Ask instead which two chapters are already doing it and whether anyone has said so out loud.

grounding.model: Diffusion of Innovations — Rogers
grounding.citation: Rogers (1962; 5th ed. 2003), Diffusion of Innovations — the adoption curve and the role of early adopters and observability.

cards.provenance: Ported 12 Sep 2026 from state-officers.html — the Early Adopter Strategy modal, the Advisor Relationship Mapping modal, and the Chapter Engagement Tracker worksheet, collapsed. Rehomed here per the salvage audit map-gap decision.

cards.title: Ask Me 3
cards.why: Three questions, asked of any provider at any appointment, turn a visit you sit through into one you understand. It is the most transferable thing in this domain — a member uses it at their own appointment, teaches it to a parent, and hands it out at a community table.

parts.heading: The three
items: What is my main problem?
What do I need to do?
Why is it important for me to do this?

parts.heading: How to use it
items: Ask them out loud. Providers are trained to answer them and most are relieved to be asked.
If the answer to the second one has more than three parts, ask which one comes first.
Write the answers down before you leave the room. Not after.

parts.heading: Teach it to one person
parts.body: The card is not learned until you have handed it to someone who will use it — a parent, a grandparent, a younger sibling. That is also what the Healthy Living portfolio scores: the ability to explain a health decision to someone else.

steps: Print the wallet card. Put it in your phone case.
Use it at your next appointment, or role-play it with a chapter partner in five minutes.
Give one card to one family member and explain why.
cards.where: Every appointment you or your family attend. Healthy Living Round Two, where explaining a personal health decision is directly scored.
cards.coach: Have members practise this on each other before they take it to a real appointment. The awkwardness is in saying it aloud the first time, not in the questions.

grounding.model: Ask Me 3 — Institute for Healthcare Improvement
grounding.citation: Ask Me 3: Good Questions for Your Good Health, developed by the Partnership for Clear Health Communication and now maintained by IHI. Practitioner tool; short enough that students use it.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Health Literacy Module HL-M1.

cards.title: Source Check
cards.why: Most health claims a member meets are in a feed, not a library. A four-question filter applied in thirty seconds is worth more than any lecture on misinformation, because it works at the moment the claim appears.

parts.heading: Four questions
items: Who published this? A person, an organisation, a company? Can you find them outside this post?
When? Health guidance changes. A date is not optional.
What are they selling? A product, a programme, a subscription, an outrage. If you cannot tell, that is the answer.
Does MedlinePlus agree? Search the topic there. If it is not there, or says something different, the claim needs more than one source before you repeat it.

parts.heading: MedlinePlus as the cross-reference
parts.body: Free, plain-language, from the National Library of Medicine, and citable. It is also the reference source for the Health Literacy Ambassador programme, so learning to reach for it does double work.

parts.heading: What to do with a claim that fails
parts.body: Do not repost. Do not argue in the comments. If it matters, take it to a chapter meeting as a Source Check example — that is a five-minute segment with no preparation.

steps: Take the last health claim you saw in a feed. Run the four questions. Time it.
Find the same topic on MedlinePlus. Note what it says differently.
Bring one failed claim to the next chapter meeting.
cards.where: Any feed, any day. Health Literacy Ambassador, which exists to counter health misinformation and uses MedlinePlus as its anchor.
cards.coach: Do not run this as a lesson about misinformation. Run it as a game — bring three claims, the chapter scores them. The filter is learned by using it, and the members who learn it teach their families.

grounding.model: Source evaluation; MedlinePlus (National Library of Medicine)
grounding.citation: MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine, as the credible-source anchor named in the Health Literacy Ambassador guideline. The four-question filter is a DC HOSA construction consistent with standard source-evaluation practice.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Health Literacy Module HL-M2 and ATC/Ambassador Module AMB-7.

cards.title: Read It, Use It
cards.why: Health literacy starts with the basic version: can you read a label, a dosage instruction, an appointment letter, and do what it says? Most members assume they can. Many cannot, on the documents that matter, and nobody has ever checked.

parts.heading: The three levels, and which one this is
parts.body: Health literacy is not one skill. It rises in three steps, and this card is the first.
items: Functional — reading and applying basic health information. A label, a dose, a notice. This card.
Interactive — extracting information and acting on it with other people. Asking a provider, helping a family member navigate a system, explaining something accurately to a peer. Lead a Team.
Critical — analysing information and using it to change the conditions that produce health. Why outcomes differ by ward, and what would move them. Lead Beyond.

parts.heading: Four documents to practise on
items: An over-the-counter medicine label. Find the dose for your age, the maximum in 24 hours, and the one thing it says not to take it with.
A prescription label. Find how many, how often, with or without food, and the refill count.
An appointment letter. Find the date, the place, what to bring, and what happens if you miss it.
A vaccine information sheet. Find what it is for, the common side effects, and who to call.

steps: Take the four documents to a chapter meeting. In pairs, find each item and time it.
Note which one took longest. That is the document type the chapter should make a handout for.
Move to Lead a Team when you can do all four in under two minutes each.
cards.where: Your own life first. Then the chapter’s health fair table, where the same documents are what people bring you.
cards.coach: This looks too basic to bother with. Run it once anyway. The members who struggle with the prescription label are the ones who will never say so, and they are the ones who most need the next card.

grounding.model: Three levels of health literacy — Nutbeam
grounding.citation: Nutbeam (2000), Health Promotion International — functional, interactive and critical health literacy.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Health Literacy Module §3 (Nutbeam ladder) at the functional level.

cards.title: Score It Before You Post It
cards.why: Every flyer, post, poster and presentation a chapter makes is patient education material. There is a validated instrument that scores such material on two things — can people understand it, and can they act on it — and it takes ten minutes. It turns ‘is this a good flyer’ from a taste argument into a number.

parts.heading: Two scores
items: Understandability — can a person of any background work out the key messages? Plain words, short sentences, one idea at a time, a clear purpose stated up front, visuals that help rather than decorate.

Actionability — can they identify what to do? A specific action, stated as a verb, with the how and the when. ‘Get screened’ is not actionable. ‘Call this number to book a free screening on Saturday’ is.

parts.heading: The gate
parts.body: Nothing the chapter produces goes out until it has been scored. Not as bureaucracy — as the one discipline that improves everything the chapter already makes without adding a single new activity.
items: Score it yourself first. Then have someone who did not make it score it. The gap between the two numbers is the finding.
Anything under the threshold you set gets one more pass. Usually the fix is cutting words and adding one sentence that starts with a verb.
Keep the scores. Six months in, the chapter can see whether its materials are getting better.

steps: Take the last thing your chapter published. Score it on the printed sheet.
Rewrite the one sentence that would most raise the actionability score.
Adopt the gate at the next officer meeting. Write it into the charter.
cards.where: Every chapter communication. Health Education, Public Service Announcement, Community Awareness — the rubrics for all three score exactly these two things. Every Level 2 Ambassador project.
cards.coach: The first time a chapter scores its own flyer, the number is usually lower than they expect and the room goes quiet. Let it. Then ask what one change would move it most. That question is the whole tool.

grounding.model: Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool — AHRQ
grounding.citation: PEMAT and User’s Guide, Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality — validated instrument scoring understandability and actionability of print and audiovisual materials.
grounding.caveat: Federal health resources have moved and been revised. Re-verify the PEMAT link and current version before distributing the printed sheet.

cards.ce: Health Education · Public Service Announcement · Health Literacy Ambassador
cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Health Literacy Module HL-O2 and ATC/Ambassador Module AMB-3.

cards.title: The Health-Literate Chapter
cards.why: Health literacy has two definitions now, and the second one is about organisations — how well they enable people to find, understand and use health information. A chapter is an organisation that produces health information. That makes it auditable, and this card is the audit.

parts.heading: Five questions, scored 1–4
parts.body: Adapted from the federal toolkit’s organisational assessment. Run in autumn, run again in spring.
items: Does our communication reach people who are not already in the room?
Can a family member who does not work in health care read our materials?
Do our events end with a next step someone can take, or do they end at awareness?
Is anything we publish available in the languages our school community speaks?
When we tell people something, do we check what they understood? (See Teach-Back.)

parts.heading: Then one improvement cycle
parts.body: Plan, do, study, act. Pick the lowest score. Decide one change. Make it. Score again. That is the whole cycle, and the second run is what turns a score into evidence.

parts.heading: The public-availability fact
parts.body: The federal toolkit this adapts is publicly available and may be reproduced without permission in the United States for non-commercial use. DC HOSA can reprint the relevant tools into chapter material directly rather than paraphrasing. Keep the AHRQ citation intact when you do.

steps: Score the five questions at an officer meeting. Do not average — the lowest number is the finding.
Choose one change for the lowest score. Name an owner and a date.
Score again after the change. Report both numbers to the chapter.
cards.where: Twice a year at officer meetings. It is also one third of the Chapter Health Literacy Challenge.
cards.coach: The multilingual question is the one chapters skip and the one that matters most in DC. If a chapter scores itself 4 on it, ask to see the translated material.

grounding.model: Organizational health literacy — Healthy People 2030; AHRQ Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit, Tool 2; PDSA
grounding.citation: Healthy People 2030 organizational health literacy definition (ODPHP). AHRQ Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit, 3rd ed. (2024), Tool 2 and the PDSA worksheet.
grounding.caveat: Re-verify federal links before distribution; the toolkit edition and location have changed before.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Health Literacy Module HL-O1.

cards.title: Teach-Back
cards.why: You do not know whether someone understood you until they say it back in their own words. Teach-back is a check on the explainer, not a quiz on the listener — which is why it is a leadership skill and not only a clinical one, and why five minutes of it at every meeting rehearses three competitive events at once.

parts.heading: The round
parts.body: Five minutes of a chapter meeting. No slides.
items: One member explains a health concept in ninety seconds. Ask Me 3, a vaccine, why hydration matters — anything from MedlinePlus.
A second member explains it back, in their own words, to the first.
The first member revises the explanation based on what did not land. That revision is the learning.

parts.heading: The phrasing that makes it work
items: Not ‘do you understand?’ — everyone says yes.
‘I want to make sure I explained that well. Can you tell me how you would describe it to someone else?’
If they cannot, the explanation failed, not the listener.

steps: Put a five-minute Teach-Back round on the next three agendas.
Rotate who explains. Nobody explains twice until everyone has once.
Keep a list of the concepts that took more than one revision — those are the chapter’s handout topics.
cards.where: Every chapter meeting. Healthy Living Round Two, Health Education and Public Service Announcement all score the ability to explain something so it lands.
cards.coach: Watch for the explainer who blames the listener. Redirect, gently and every time: what would you change in what you said? That reframe is the entire point.

grounding.model: Teach-back method — AHRQ Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit, Tool 5
grounding.citation: AHRQ Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit, 3rd ed. (2024), Tool 5: Use the Teach-Back Method.

cards.ce: Healthy Living · Health Education · Public Service Announcement
cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Health Literacy Module HL-O3. Also the practical home of the Voice · Lead a Team topic ‘Explain it so it lands’.

cards.title: Become an Ambassador
cards.why: Health Literacy Ambassador is the only event in the catalogue every member in every division can complete, with no entry cap and no ranking, and Level 1 ends with the member delivering a presentation at a chapter meeting. That means every ambassador generates chapter programming as a side effect. It is a participation programme wearing an event’s clothes, and the chapters that treat it that way get a year of meetings written for free.

parts.heading: Level 1
items: Complete the online module. A certificate and Level 2 access instructions arrive by email.
Build a presentation on a MedlinePlus health topic — length, content and style are the member’s choice.
Deliver it at a chapter meeting or in class. That delivery is the chapter’s meeting segment.

parts.heading: Level 2
items: Complete the virtual escape-room module — MedlinePlus-based puzzles. Members may work in a small group, but each needs their own computer and submits for their own certificate.

Complete one of five projects using MedlinePlus: posters for a physician’s office · an article for the Chartered Association newsletter · materials for a career, senior, clinic or hospital fair · patient handouts for professionals or employers · educational tips shared with others.
Present the project to peers. Upload the presentation and supporting documents as one combined PDF — new for 2026–27; the old activity-tracking system is no longer used.

parts.heading: The access checklist — this is what decides whether it happens
parts.body: The friction is invisible from outside and decisive inside a DC classroom.
items: Certificates are emailed, and many school email systems block external senders. Every participant needs a working personal email address before starting. Some will not have one — find out first.
Level 1 needs a laptop or Chromebook. It switches between two sites; a phone will not work.
Level 2 needs guest sign-in and one computer per member, even in a group.
Run Level 1 as a whole-chapter session in a booked computer lab, not as homework. This single decision is the highest-leverage one in the whole programme.

parts.heading: The window
parts.body: Activities from 1 June 2026 to 15 May 2027 count for international recognition. DC HOSA sets its own deadline and recognition method for Chartered Association recognition — until that is published, members default to the international window.

steps: Book the computer lab. Confirm every participant has a personal email that receives external mail.
Run Level 1 as one session. Schedule the resulting presentations across the year’s meetings — one or two per meeting, with a sign-up board and a topic register so no two members build the same topic.
Score every Level 2 project on the PEMAT sheet before it goes anywhere.
cards.where: Chapter meetings all year. Every Level 2 project is patient education material, which is the Community Awareness and Public Service Announcement rubric in practice.
cards.coach: The access checklist is the advisor’s job and it is the entire difference between a chapter with fifteen ambassadors and a chapter with two. A member who wants to do this and does not have a personal email or a laptop at home simply does not complete it, and nobody finds out why.

grounding.model: Health Literacy Ambassador ILC Guidelines 2026–27; expectancy-value cost term
grounding.citation: Health Literacy Ambassador ILC Guidelines, September 2026, hosa.org (NLM-sponsored). The access barriers are the cost term of Expectancy-Value Theory (Eccles & Wigfield) applied literally.
grounding.caveat: Guideline mechanics — upload method, module platforms, deadlines — are as published for 2026–27 and are revised mid-season. Re-pull before promoting.
