cards.title: Map Your Ward
cards.why: A poster in the school hallway reaches the people who are already reached. The organisations in your ward that do health outreach — clinics, libraries, faith communities, recreation centres, mutual aid — already hold the community’s trust. Health literacy work done alongside them reaches people a school-based event never will.

parts.heading: Who to map
parts.body: One page, one ward. Name, what they do, who they reach, a contact, and whether the chapter has ever spoken to them.
items: Community clinics and health centres.
Public library branches — they run programmes and have display space.
Faith communities with health ministries or regular gatherings.
Recreation centres and senior centres.
Mutual aid groups and neighbourhood associations.
The ward’s Advisory Neighborhood Commission — it knows who else is doing what.

parts.heading: What the map is for
items: Level 2 Ambassador projects need a place — a physician’s office, a fair, a clinic. The map is the venue list.
The advocacy Audience element: a chapter that wants to be heard needs to know who is already listening in the ward.
Partnerships that outlive this year’s officers, because the map is written down.

steps: Fill the printed map for your ward. Six organisations minimum.
Pick one the chapter has never contacted. Write the one-sentence ask.
Put the map in the Transition Packet so next year’s officers start with it.
cards.where: Before any community event. Every Level 2 Ambassador placement. The One-Page Ask at Voice · Lead Beyond.
cards.coach: Chapters default to the school hallway because it needs no permission. Ask what the chapter’s ward is, then ask for one organisation in it by name. If the answer takes more than five seconds, the map does not exist yet.

grounding.model: Community asset mapping; Lundy Model — Audience
grounding.citation: Community partner mapping as a practitioner convention. The Audience element from the Lundy Model of Participation (R) is the reason it matters.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Health Literacy Module HL-O4 and ATC/Ambassador Module AMB-4.

cards.title: Healthy Living, Run Deliberately
cards.why: Healthy Living asks a member to set a personal health goal, sustain it for months, and present the journey. Framed as behaviour change and self-advocacy — which is what the rubric scores — it is one of the best events in the catalogue. Framed around weight or body, it is the wrong container for a teenager, and the guideline itself says so. The framing is a choice, and it is the chapter’s to make.

parts.heading: What the event actually rewards
items: A specific goal, a baseline taken before the goal period starts, and evidence of sustained effort — the top scoring band asks for nine to twelve months.
A five-minute presentation that integrates the portfolio rather than reading from it.
The three published sample goals are daily hydration, a running time, and reducing stress headaches through a short daily practice. None is a weight goal. That is the intended framing.

parts.heading: Goals that work
parts.body: Behaviour or capacity, never body size.
items: ‘Drink water instead of soda at lunch, every school day.’
‘Run a mile without stopping by March.’
‘Sleep before 11 on school nights, four nights a week.’
‘Ten minutes of the breathing practice before every test.’

parts.heading: How to promote it
items: As a behaviour-change and self-advocacy event.
Never with before-and-after framing, body imagery, or language that ranks bodies.
The goal window opened 1 July 2026 and runs to 15 May 2027 — members are already inside it.

steps: Write your goal as a behaviour with a frequency. If it contains a number about your body, rewrite it.
Take the baseline before the first day, and discuss it with a licensed provider if the goal involves diet or exercise.
Bring the goal to your advisor for the required signature, and expect them to read it.
cards.where: Healthy Living Round Two. Also the member-facing half of the Ask Me 3 and Teach-Back cards, since explaining the journey is what is scored.
cards.coach: The advisor signature is a review, not a formality, and it is the event’s main safety mechanism. A goal framed around weight, body size or restriction gets redirected to a behaviour goal before it is signed — the guideline gives you the standing to do that. A member showing distress around food, exercise or body image is routed to the school counsellor and their family and is not steered into this event; a competitive frame around personal health is the wrong container for that student. Portfolio review happens before submission with the student choosing what stays in, and the permission form is signed by a parent or guardian, not collected at the registration table. Quote the guideline’s own guardrails when briefing other advisors — it explicitly discourages any diet or exercise programme not under a licensed provider’s direction.

grounding.model: Healthy Living ILC Guidelines 2026–27; behaviour-change framing
grounding.citation: Healthy Living ILC Guidelines, September 2026 (2026–27), hosa.org, NASM-sponsored — event mechanics, sample goals, and the guideline’s own safeguarding language.
grounding.caveat: Event mechanics are as published for 2026–27. One published sample question references a ‘Supplementation’ module that does not appear in the five-band test plan; resolve against the NASM course before building any test preparation, which belongs to the Study Hub in any case.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Health Literacy Module §1–2 and HL-A1. Safeguarding material placed in the coach note, per the module’s instruction to keep it out of student-facing text.

cards.title: The Ward Lens
cards.why: Health outcomes in DC differ sharply from one ward to the next. Knowing that is not the skill. The skill is moving from ‘this ward has worse outcomes’ to the determinants behind it and the decisions that produced them — and then to the one decision a chapter or an affiliate could actually influence. That is the critical level of health literacy, and it is the level a state officer should be modelling.

parts.heading: Start with the published data, not with a story
parts.body: DC Health publishes ward-level health data. Use the current release, cite it, and date it. Do not carry a figure from memory or from this card — the numbers move and this card deliberately holds none.
items: Pick one outcome. Life expectancy, a chronic condition, access to a provider, a screening rate.
Find it by ward in the current DC Health data. Write down the source and the year.
Find the ward where it is worst and the ward where it is best.

parts.heading: Then ask what produces the gap
parts.body: Determinants, not behaviour. The question is never ‘what are people in that ward doing wrong’.
items: Where are the providers, the pharmacies, the grocery stores, the clinics — and how long does it take to reach them without a car?
What does housing, income, and school quality look like, and how long has it looked that way?
Which past decisions — zoning, transit, hospital closures, where a clinic was built — shaped the current map?
Which of those is a decision someone could still make differently?

parts.heading: Then choose the one thing
parts.body: A chapter cannot fix a determinant. It can pick one, in one ward, and act on it — a health fair placed where the map says it is needed, a One-Page Ask to the Council about one specific gap, a partnership with the one organisation already working on it.

steps: Choose one outcome and find it by ward in current DC Health data. Cite it.
List three determinants that plausibly produce the gap. For each, name a decision that shaped it.
Write the one thing your chapter or the SEC could do about one of them, this year.
cards.where: SEC strategic planning. The Community domain’s highest level, and the determinants layer under World Health & Disparities and Public Health.
cards.coach: Two failure modes. The first is stopping at the disparity — it feels like insight and it is only a fact. The second is blaming behaviour. When an officer says a ward has worse outcomes ‘because people there…’, stop them and ask what is within a mile of that person’s home.

grounding.model: Critical health literacy — Nutbeam; social determinants of health
grounding.citation: Nutbeam (2000) critical level. Social determinants framework per Healthy People 2030 and the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health. Data: DC Health, current ward-level publications — cite the specific release used.
grounding.caveat: This card contains no figures on purpose. Any number a member uses must come from a named, dated DC Health source.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Health Literacy Module HL-S1.

cards.title: Organizational Health Literacy
cards.why: The second definition of health literacy is about the organisation, not the person: how well it enables people to find, understand and use health information. It applies to DC HOSA exactly as it applies to a chapter. A Chartered Association that tells chapters to communicate clearly while sending dense advisor emails has an organisational health literacy problem of its own, and this is how you find out.

parts.heading: The two definitions
parts.body: Healthy People 2030 split the old single definition in two and shifted the emphasis from understanding to use, and from the individual to the organisation.
items: Personal — the degree to which individuals can find, understand and use information and services to inform health decisions for themselves and others.
Organisational — the degree to which organisations equitably enable individuals to do the same.

parts.heading: Run the chapter audit on the affiliate
parts.body: The five questions from The Health-Literate Chapter, applied to DC HOSA itself.
items: The website. Can a parent new to CTSOs work out what HOSA is and what it costs in under two minutes?
Advisor communications. Score the last three emails on the PEMAT sheet.
Conference materials. Is there a next step someone can take, or does it end at information?
Family-facing content. In which languages?
Recognition programmes. Can a member find out how to qualify without asking someone?

parts.heading: Adopt a plain-language standard
parts.body: Federal plain-language guidance exists and is free. Adopting it as a house standard for affiliate communication is a decision the SEC and state staff can make in one meeting, and it costs nothing.

steps: Score the affiliate on the five questions. Publish the scores to the SEC.
Fix the lowest one this term. Name an owner.
Propose the plain-language standard as a Standing Rule.
cards.where: SEC and state staff planning. It is also the third of the three parts of the Chapter Health Literacy Challenge — the affiliate has to have done it before asking chapters to.
cards.coach: If the SEC proposes the challenge to chapters before running the audit on the affiliate, stop them. Nothing undermines a health literacy campaign faster than an unreadable email announcing it.

grounding.model: Organizational health literacy — Healthy People 2030; plain language (federal standard)
grounding.citation: Healthy People 2030 definitions of personal and organizational health literacy (ODPHP). Federal plain-language guidelines, plainlanguage.gov.
grounding.caveat: Re-verify federal links before adopting the standard formally; federal health and plain-language resources have moved.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Health Literacy Module §3 (spine), HL-S3 and HL-T1.

cards.title: The Chapter Health Literacy Challenge
cards.why: A state-level campaign that every chapter can complete cheaply, that produces affiliate-level evidence rather than an attendance count, and that ties directly to the recognition ladder chapters already care about. It is three existing cards run once each, reported once, and recognised.

parts.heading: The three parts, per chapter
items: Run The Health-Literate Chapter audit once. Report the lowest score.
Score one piece of chapter material on the PEMAT sheet. Report the score and one change made.
Set a participation proportion for Health Literacy Ambassador Level 1 — the share of members completing it by a stated date. A proportion, not a count, so it is fair across chapters of every size.

parts.heading: Recognition
parts.body: International HOSA awards no medals for Ambassador. The Chartered Association recognition carries all the motivational weight, and the State Advisor sets it.
items: Tie Ambassador participation to the Standards of Excellence ladder — Emerging, Established, Elite — as one of the criteria that moves a chapter up a tier. That gives the ladder a behaviour to reward.
Recognise at SLC, by chapter name. A named cohort in affiliate communications. A banner.
Publish the DC deadline and the recognition method before launch. Until they exist, chapters default to the international window and the campaign has no forcing date.

parts.heading: What the SEC gets back
parts.body: An affiliate-wide dataset: lowest audit scores by chapter, PEMAT scores before and after, Ambassador participation rates. That is something evidence-based to say about the affiliate at the end of the year.

steps: Run the affiliate-level audit first (Organizational Health Literacy). Do not skip this.
Publish the DC Ambassador deadline and the recognition method. Both are State Advisor decisions.
Launch with two or three early-adopter chapters. Make their result visible. Then the rest.
cards.where: The SEC calendar, launched in autumn so the Ambassador window is used. Reported at SLC.
cards.coach: This is the one campaign in the Hub where the state staff decisions — deadline, recognition — gate everything. Make them before the SEC designs the launch, or the SEC will design around their absence.

grounding.model: Chapter-level health literacy campaign; Diffusion of Innovations for rollout
grounding.citation: DC HOSA construction combining three R-graded instruments (organizational audit, PEMAT, Ambassador guideline). Rollout sequencing per Rogers (R). Standards of Excellence tiers as settled 7 Sep 2026.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Health Literacy Module HL-S2 and ATC/Ambassador Module AMB-1, AMB-5, §8.

cards.title: What a Team Expects of You
cards.why: A chapter that works has written down what its members owe each other — how fast people reply, how a disagreement gets raised, what happens when someone misses a commitment. As a member you did not write that document, but you are bound by it, and the fastest way to be trusted with more is to know it and keep it.

parts.heading: Ask to see it
parts.body: Every chapter with an officer charter has a member-facing half. If yours does not, ask an officer what the unwritten version is. The answer tells you a lot about the chapter.

parts.heading: The four that matter most
items: Response time. If the group chat expects a reply within a day, a reply within a day. Silence reads as absence.
Commitments. If you say you will do a thing, it happens or you say early that it will not. Late is recoverable; silent is not.
Disagreement. Raise it to the person, in the way the charter says, not around them.
Showing up. Two meetings missed without a word is a signal to the officers whether you mean it as one or not.

parts.heading: What you get back
parts.body: A chapter that keeps these is one where you get a real task with a real deadline by your third meeting — because you have shown you will do it. That is the trade.

steps: Read the chapter charter, or ask an officer to describe the expectations in one minute.
Pick the one of the four you are weakest on. Fix that one this month.
Reply to the next chapter message within the day, even if the reply is ‘can’t, sorry’.
cards.where: Your first month in the chapter. It is the member side of the Officer Charter at Lead a Team.
cards.coach: Members are rarely told what is expected until they have already broken it. Have officers read the member-facing half of the charter aloud at the first meeting of the year. Once.

grounding.model: Team charters — Mathieu & Rapp
grounding.citation: Mathieu & Rapp (2009), Journal of Applied Psychology 94(1), 90–103 — teams with high-quality charters showed better performance trajectories. This card is the member-facing corollary.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Rebuild Specification §3 Team L1.

cards.title: Say the Uncomfortable Thing
cards.why: Teams that work are ones where people can say ‘I think this is wrong’, ‘I don’t know how to do this’, or ‘I made a mistake’ without paying for it. That condition has a name, it is the strongest single predictor of team effectiveness there is, and it is created by what the person in charge does — not by team-building activities.

parts.heading: What it is
parts.body: Psychological safety: the shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking. Not niceness. Not the absence of disagreement. The opposite — a team where disagreement is cheap enough to happen.

parts.heading: As a member, three things you can do
items: Ask the question everyone is thinking. The first person to say ‘I don’t understand the plan’ makes it possible for the next four.
Report your own mistake before it is found. Early and plainly. ‘I dropped this, here is where it stands.’
When someone else does either of those, respond to the content and not to the courage. Treat it as normal, because it should be.

parts.heading: How the chapter measures it
parts.body: There is a seven-item scale, free and short. Officers run it in October and again in March and report the team average — never individual answers. If the number is low, the fix is in what the officers do, not in the members.

steps: At the next meeting, ask one question you would normally keep to yourself.
The next time you drop something, say so in the group chat within the day.
Answer the seven-item pulse honestly when the officers send it.
cards.where: Every meeting, every group chat. The Debrief card depends on it entirely.
cards.coach: You cannot instruct a team to be safe. You can only go first — state your own mistake before anyone else speaks, respond to a hard question with thanks rather than defence, and do it every time. The seven-item pulse tells you whether it is working; the members’ behaviour tells you whether you are.

grounding.model: Psychological safety — Edmondson
grounding.citation: Edmondson (1999), Administrative Science Quarterly — the construct and the seven-item team psychological safety scale. Identified as the strongest predictor of team effectiveness in Google’s Project Aristotle.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Content Research Map §3.3 at the member level; the Seven-Item Pulse instrument referenced here and administered from the Officer Charter card.

cards.title: When Someone Is Upset
cards.why: Saying the wrong thing to someone in distress does not just fail to help — it tells them their experience is invalid, and trust closes in seconds. In a clinic that costs a patient relationship; in a chapter it costs a member. These are questions that open the conversation instead of closing it.

parts.heading: Ask this, not that
items: Anger — ask ‘what boundary do you feel was crossed?’ Not ‘calm down’ or ‘it’s not a big deal’.
Sadness — ask ‘what loss or unmet expectation is this?’ Not ‘it could be worse’.
Anxiety — ask ‘what worries you most, and what is actually in your control?’ Not ‘just relax’.
Frustration — ask ‘what is at stake that you care about?’ Not ‘let it go’.
Overwhelm — ask ‘what is one thing we could take off your plate right now?’ Not ‘everyone’s busy’.
Shame — ask ‘what story are you telling yourself about what happened?’ Not ‘you shouldn’t feel that way’.
Fear — ask ‘what is the worst that could realistically happen, and could you handle it?’ Not ‘don’t be scared’.
Disappointment — ask ‘what were you expecting that didn’t happen?’ Not ‘you should have known’.

parts.heading: The pattern under all eight
parts.body: Every ‘ask’ line is a question about the person’s experience. Every ‘not’ line is an instruction to stop having it. That is the whole difference, and it is enough.

steps: Pick the one emotion you most often meet in the chapter. Learn its ‘ask’ line by heart.
The next time you catch yourself about to say a ‘not’ line, ask the question instead.
Notice what happens in the following ten seconds.
cards.where: After a competition result. In the group chat at 11pm. At a health fair table when someone is scared of what they just read.
cards.coach: This is a script, not a theory, and it is labelled as one. It works because it is specific and rehearsed. Do not let it become a poster — have members practise the lines in pairs once, out loud.

grounding.model: Practitioner script for responding to negative emotions
grounding.citation: Practitioner framework as supplied in the original DC HOSA materials. Consistent with the validation literature in clinical communication, but the specific eight-line script has no independent empirical base — present it as a working tool, never as research.

cards.provenance: Ported 12 Sep 2026 from members.html ‘Supporting Others’ Emotions’ modal. Relabelled P per the salvage audit.

cards.title: Write the Charter
cards.why: Charter-writing is one of the few team interventions with clean evidence behind it. It costs one meeting in the first two weeks, and officer teams almost never do it — then spend the year having the arguments the charter would have settled.

parts.heading: Six fields, one page, signed
items: What this team exists to accomplish this year. One or two sentences, not a mission statement.
Who decides what, and by what rule — consensus, majority, the president’s call. Name the rule per type of decision.
Expected response time on the group chat.
How we raise a disagreement. To whom, in what form, by when.
What happens the first time someone misses a commitment. Written before it happens, so it is a procedure and not a confrontation.
When we revisit this document. The date. This field is what separates a charter from a poster.

parts.heading: Add the accountability script
parts.body: The last field of the charter is the exact wording one officer uses to raise a missed commitment with another. Agreed in advance, it is usable. Improvised in the moment, it is a conflict. See Hold a Peer Accountable.

parts.heading: Run the pulse from it
parts.body: The seven-item psychological safety scale goes out in October and March. The charter names who sends it and states that only the team average is reported.

steps: Book one officer meeting in the first two weeks of the term for nothing but this.
Fill all six fields. Sign it. Photograph it.
Put the revisit date in the calendar — the January reset is the natural one.
cards.where: The first two weeks of every officer term, at chapter and state level. Revisited at the January midpoint.
cards.coach: If a team says they ‘don’t need’ a charter because they get along, that is the team that needs it most — they have never had the disagreement that would have tested it. Ask what happens the first time someone misses a deadline. If nobody can answer in a sentence, there is no charter.

grounding.model: Team charters and performance strategies — Mathieu & Rapp
grounding.citation: Mathieu & Rapp (2009), Journal of Applied Psychology 94(1), 90–103.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Content Research Map §3.2 and Audience Tool Addendum S1, S6.

cards.title: Conflict Triage
cards.why: Conflict on a team comes in three kinds, and the wrong response to one kind makes it worse. Before responding to any officer-team conflict, the chair answers one question — which kind is this — and that answer routes to a different script. The single most useful move a student leader can learn is converting a relationship complaint into a task or process question.

parts.heading: The three kinds
items: Task — what are we doing? A disagreement about the goal, the event, the decision. Some of this is healthy.
Process — how are we doing it? Who decides, who does what, by when. Usually a charter gap.
Relationship — how do we feel about each other. Consistently harmful, and it is never resolved in a meeting.

parts.heading: Three scripts
items: Task → structured debate. Put both positions on the board, give each side two minutes uninterrupted, vote or decide by the rule in the charter.
Process → charter amendment. The conflict is a missing rule. Write the rule; the conflict usually dissolves.
Relationship → a private conversation between the two people, or with the chair as a third. Not the group chat, not the meeting. Ever.

parts.heading: The conversion
parts.body: Most relationship complaints have a task or process complaint underneath. ‘She never listens’ is often ‘she made a decision the charter says we make together’. Find the underneath and treat that.

steps: Next conflict: before responding, write down which of the three it is.
Apply the matching script and nothing else.
If it was relationship, ask what the task or process complaint underneath might be.
cards.where: Officer team meetings. SEC. Any committee. It replaces the difficult-conversations models the old build carried.
cards.coach: Advisors get pulled into relationship conflict and try to mediate it in front of the team. Do not. Take it private, and ask each person separately what the other one did — the task or process answer is usually right there.

grounding.model: Task, relationship and process conflict — Jehn; De Dreu & Weingart meta-analysis
grounding.citation: Jehn (1995), Administrative Science Quarterly; De Dreu & Weingart (2003), Journal of Applied Psychology — relationship conflict consistently harmful, task conflict less benign than earlier claimed. Interest-based framing after Fisher & Ury (P).

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Content Research Map §3.5. Replaces the ALIGN / CALM ‘Difficult Conversations’ modal from advisors.html (salvage audit: REWRITE).

cards.title: Hand Off a Task
cards.why: Delegation fails in one of two ways: the task is thrown over the wall and dropped, or it is handed over and then taken back at the first wobble. There is a four-rung sequence that avoids both, and health science students already know it — it is how a clinical skill is taught.

parts.heading: Four rungs
parts.body: Same task, four passes, the officer stepping back one rung each time.
items: You do it while they watch. Narrate what you are deciding, not just what you are doing.
You do it together. They drive, you are beside them.
They do it while you watch. You say nothing unless asked.
They do it and report back. You are not in the room.

parts.heading: What each rung is for
items: Rung one makes the invisible decisions visible.
Rung two catches the misunderstanding before it becomes a habit.
Rung three is the hard one for the officer — the silence is the teaching.
Rung four is the only rung that counts as delegation. The first three are training.

parts.heading: Not this
parts.body: The old build carried a matrix that matched a leadership ‘style’ to a member’s readiness. That model is widely taught and has weak evidence for the prescribed matching. Retired. The four rungs are simpler, and they work.

steps: Pick one task you keep doing yourself. Name the member who should own it by December.
Schedule the four rungs on four dates.
On rung three, say nothing. Time yourself.
cards.where: Every officer who does too much. The advisor side of it is the Student-Led Transfer Ladder — which chapter functions the advisor still performs that a student could.
cards.coach: The rung most officers skip is three. They go from doing it together to handing it over, and the member fails, and the officer concludes delegation does not work. Ask which rung they are on. It is nearly always two.

grounding.model: Graduated handoff; expert coaching condition — Hackman
grounding.citation: Hackman’s expert-coaching condition rendered as a four-step progression; parallels the see-one/do-one clinical skills sequence. Replaces Situational Leadership (Hersey & Blanchard), grade C — heavily taught, weak empirical support for style-matching.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Audience Tool Addendum O5 and A4. Replaces the ‘Student Empowerment Matrix’ modal from advisors.html (salvage audit: REWRITE, retired model).

cards.title: Give Feedback That Lands
cards.why: Feedback is the thing a chapter officer does most often and is taught least. One three-part structure — what happened, what the person did, what effect it had — keeps it specific enough to act on and free of the judgement that makes people stop listening.

parts.heading: Situation, behaviour, impact
items: Situation — when and where. ‘At Tuesday’s meeting, during the fundraiser discussion.’
Behaviour — what they did, observably. ‘You cut in three times while Sam was talking.’ Not ‘you were rude’.
Impact — what it did. ‘Sam stopped contributing and we lost the one person who had run a fundraiser.’

parts.heading: Then stop
parts.body: Do not add advice unless asked. The three parts are the feedback; the next step is theirs to propose. If they ask, offer one thing, not five.

parts.heading: It works in both directions
parts.body: The same three parts deliver praise that is worth something. ‘At the health fair, you stayed with the grandmother who was frightened by her results, and she left with a plan. That is the whole reason we were there.’

steps: Write the next piece of feedback you need to give in the three parts before you give it.
Delete every adjective about the person. Keep every verb about the behaviour.
Give one piece of positive feedback this week in the same three parts.
cards.where: After every event. In every one-to-one. It is the everyday tool that Conflict Triage and Hold a Peer Accountable escalate from.
cards.coach: Officers give feedback as a character judgement because it is faster. Ask them to say the behaviour line first, before anything else. If they cannot name a behaviour, there is no feedback yet — only a feeling.

grounding.model: Situation–Behavior–Impact — Center for Creative Leadership
grounding.citation: SBI feedback model, Center for Creative Leadership. Widely used practitioner tool; label it as such.

cards.provenance: Ported 12 Sep 2026 from officers.html SBI Feedback Card. Rehomed here per the salvage audit map-gap decision — feedback was absent from the topic map.

cards.title: Fill the Room
cards.why: Recruitment is a funnel with five stages, and at every stage people leave for a reason. The reason is almost never the message. It is a cost — a meeting time that collides with a bus route, a dues figure nobody explained, a first meeting where everyone else already knew each other. Find the cost at each stage and the funnel fills itself.

parts.heading: Five stages, each with a conversion action and a cost
items: Hears about it → attends once. Action: a named person invites them. Cost: they do not know anyone who will be there.
Attends once → joins. Action: they are given something to do before they leave. Cost: dues, and nobody said what they buy.
Joins → engages. Action: a real task with a deadline by meeting three. Cost: the meeting time, the location, the transport.
Engages → leads. Action: the four-rung handoff of one function. Cost: fear of being the only one who cares.
Leads → recruits. Action: they invite the next one, by name.

parts.heading: The cost column is the point
parts.body: For every stage, write the cost in time, money, social risk and what the member gives up to be there. Most chapters have never written that column. When they do, the fix is nearly always logistics, not messaging.

parts.heading: The first thirty days
parts.body: Onboarding is the second and third stage done deliberately. One named action per week — a greeting by name at meeting one; a real task by meeting three; a question about what they want from HOSA before week four, with a promise about how the answer will be used.

steps: Fill the five-stage funnel for your chapter on the printed sheet. Cost column first.
Pick the stage where most people leave. Change one cost.
Write the first-thirty-days sequence and assign one officer to run it for every new member.
cards.where: August to October. Again in January for the second-semester intake.
cards.coach: When a chapter says nobody comes, ask what time the meeting is and how the members get home. That is usually the answer, and it has nothing to do with the flyer.

grounding.model: Expectancy-Value Theory, cost term — Eccles & Wigfield; Developmental Relationships Framework — Search Institute
grounding.citation: Eccles & Wigfield expectancy-value model, the cost term. Search Institute Developmental Relationships Framework — express care, challenge growth, provide support, share power, expand possibilities — for the first-thirty-days sequence.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Audience Tool Addendum O4 and Content Research Map §3.4 (First Thirty Days), combined.

cards.title: Five Conditions
cards.why: Most chapters that say they have a motivation problem have a structure problem. There are five conditions under which teams work, and scoring them in September and again in January tells you which one is missing — and each missing one routes to a different fix. This replaces the stage model most leadership material still teaches.

parts.heading: Five questions, scored 1–4
items: A real team — is membership stable and bounded? Does everyone know who is on it?
A compelling direction — can every officer say in one sentence what the year is for?
An enabling structure — are roles clear, are meetings designed, is the work divided so it can actually be done?
A supportive context — does the chapter have the room, the budget, the advisor time, the school’s backing?
Expert coaching — is someone helping the team get better at working together, not only at the task?

parts.heading: Low score, different fix
items: Low direction → a goal-setting problem. Write the one sentence.
Low structure → a roles-and-meetings problem. Charter and agenda.
Low context → an advocacy problem. The Internal Advocacy Pack goes to an administrator.
Low coaching → an advisor problem, or a state-staff one.
Low ‘real team’ → the roster is the problem. Who is actually on this?

parts.heading: What was retired
parts.body: Forming, storming, norming, performing is universally taught and has never held up as a sequence teams pass through. Keep the four words as vocabulary if they help. Do not diagnose a chapter with them.

steps: Score the five in September at an officer meeting. Do not average.
Take the lowest and apply its fix.
Score again in January. Whether the number moved is the finding.
cards.where: Chapter officer teams and the SEC, twice a year. The affiliate-level version is the health record state staff keep per chapter.
cards.coach: Chapters diagnose themselves with the wrong word. ‘We have no motivation’ is nearly always a 1 on structure. Run the five questions before accepting any chapter’s own diagnosis.

grounding.model: Conditions for team effectiveness — Hackman
grounding.citation: Hackman (2002), Leading Teams — real team, compelling direction, enabling structure, supportive context, expert coaching. Replaces Tuckman’s stage model, grade C.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Content Research Map §3.1. Replaces the Chapter Health Diagnostic from advisors.html (salvage audit: REWRITE).

cards.title: The January Reset
cards.why: Teams do not improve gradually. They change sharply at the temporal midpoint of their lifespan, when the deadline suddenly becomes real. An officer term runs September to May; the midpoint is January. A reset scheduled there is not generic advice — it is the one moment the research says a team is most willing to change how it works.

parts.heading: What the midpoint does
parts.body: Around halfway, a team realises how much time is left and how much of the plan has not happened. That realisation is uncomfortable and it is useful — it is the only point in the year when a team will voluntarily abandon its September assumptions.

parts.heading: The reset, in one meeting
items: Re-score the Five Conditions. Compare to September.
Re-read the charter. Amend what has not held.
Each officer writes a midpoint memo: what I said I would do, what has happened, what I am changing for the second half. One page.
Re-derive the calendar from the second peak — the offsite Round Two dates and SLC.
One decision the team has been avoiding, decided.

parts.heading: For the SEC
parts.body: This is the defensible reason for a mid-year retreat. Not a reward, not a bonding exercise — the point in the year when the council is most able to change course.

steps: Put the reset in the calendar now, in the first two weeks of January, before anything else claims the date.
Send the midpoint memo template two weeks before.
Run the five parts in order. The avoided decision goes last so it cannot be skipped.
cards.where: January, every year, at every level. It is also the second reading of the charter and the second run of the Five Conditions.
cards.coach: The reset fails when it is run as a celebration. Open with the September scores and the calendar as it actually stands. Let the gap be visible before anyone talks about what went well.

grounding.model: Punctuated equilibrium in groups — Gersick
grounding.citation: Gersick (1988), Academy of Management Journal — teams shift sharply at the temporal midpoint of their lifespan rather than improving gradually.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Content Research Map §3.1 and Audience Tool Addendum S5.

cards.title: Hold a Peer Accountable
cards.why: Raising a missed commitment with a peer is the hardest conversation on an officer team, because nobody outranks anybody. The only thing that makes it possible is agreeing the exact words in advance and writing them into the charter. Decided before it is needed, it is a procedure. Decided in the moment, it is a fight.

parts.heading: The script, written in September
parts.body: The charter states it. Something like:
items: ‘You said you would have X by Y. It is not here. Where does it stand, and what do you need?’
The three parts: the commitment as it was made, the fact that it was not kept, an open question. No adjectives. No history.
The reply is also scripted: a status, and a new date or a request for help. Not an explanation of why.

parts.heading: Why it works
parts.body: Because it was agreed. The person raising it is doing what the team decided, not making a personal accusation. The person receiving it heard the words in September and signed them.

parts.heading: The second time
parts.body: The charter also says what happens the second time. Usually: the task moves to someone else, stated in the meeting, without discussion. That is not punishment. It is what the team agreed.

steps: Write the exact script into the charter at the first officer meeting. Read it aloud.
The first time it is needed, use the words as written. Do not improve them.
Debrief afterwards, privately, with the person — how did the script land.
cards.where: Officer teams and the SEC, from the second month onward. It is the last field of Write the Charter.
cards.coach: When an officer tells you a teammate is not pulling their weight, ask whether the script has been used. It almost never has. Do not run the conversation for them; ask them to run it as written and report back.

grounding.model: Psychological safety; team charters
grounding.citation: Edmondson (1999) on the conditions under which peers can raise problems; Mathieu & Rapp (2009) on charters as the vehicle for pre-agreed norms.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Audience Tool Addendum S6.

cards.title: Force Field
cards.why: Every change a team tries to make has forces pushing it forward and forces holding it back. The instinct is to push harder. The finding is that pushing harder often increases the resistance too. The sustainable path is usually to reduce a restraining force — simplify the form, move the date — rather than to shout louder for compliance.

parts.heading: Map both sides
parts.body: One page. The change you want across the top. Driving forces on the left, restraining on the right, each rated weak, medium, or strong.
items: Example — every chapter submitting officer applications on time. Driving: SEC visibility, peer chapters submitting early, the benefit of more planning time, advisor buy-in. Restraining: competing school deadlines, a confusing form, advisor turnover, no consequence for lateness historically.

parts.heading: Then choose
items: Which restraining force is easiest to reduce? Usually process friction — the form, the timing, the instructions.
Which driving force is most worth strengthening? Usually visibility of early adopters.
Do one of each. Not everything.

parts.heading: Where it fits
parts.body: Run it before the January reset on the change the team most needs to make in the second half. Run it before any statewide initiative, as the first page of the launch plan.

steps: Name the change. Fill both columns on the printed sheet.
Rate each force.
Pick one restraining force to reduce and one driving force to strengthen. Assign each.
cards.where: Before any change the team is about to push for. It pairs with Early Adopters First at Governance · Lead Beyond.
cards.coach: Teams fill the driving column enthusiastically and leave the restraining column half empty. Make them fill the right side first. The right side is where the plan is.

grounding.model: Force field analysis — Lewin
grounding.citation: Lewin (1951), Field Theory in Social Science. A classic practitioner tool with theoretical grounding; the specific driving/restraining analysis is not an empirically validated intervention and is labelled accordingly.

cards.provenance: Ported 12 Sep 2026 from state-officers.html — Force Field Analysis section and worksheet. Rehomed here per the salvage audit map-gap decision; regraded P.

cards.title: Know Your Strengths
cards.why: Most strengths tools give you a label. One gives you a list of sixty specific things a student leader can do, sorted into eight clusters, with a free inventory built for young people. A list that specific is something you can write a goal against. A label is not.

parts.heading: The eight clusters
parts.body: Sixty competencies sit inside these. Each one is defined on four dimensions — do you know it, do you value it, can you do it, do you actually do it.
items: Learning and reasoning · Self-awareness and development · Group dynamics · Interpersonal interaction · Civic responsibility · Communication · Strategic planning · Personal behaviour

parts.heading: Take the inventory
items: The Student Leadership Competencies Inventory is free, has a shortened youth version, and takes about twenty minutes.
Results are not stored. Print or screenshot them before closing the page — you will need them in April.
A separate free 360 evaluation measures the behaviour dimension — what others see you do. That one comes later.

parts.heading: What to do with sixty
parts.body: Nothing, yet. The point of this card is the vocabulary. The next card picks two.

parts.heading: Why this maps to the pillars
parts.body: The eight clusters sit cleanly under BUILD, EMPOWER, ADVANCE and CONNECT. That gives every card in this Hub and every module in the Advisor Development Program a common language.

steps: Take the youth inventory. Save the results somewhere you will find in April.
Read the eight cluster names aloud. Pick the one that surprised you.
Move to Two Competencies, One Term when you have the results in hand.
cards.where: September, for every member. It is the measurement spine’s first instrument — September and April.
cards.coach: The other tools members will have met — personality types, learning styles, strengths labels — have been retired from this Hub for weak evidence and because they teach members to explain problems as fixed traits. If a member arrives with one of those, do not argue; hand them this inventory and ask which two competencies they want to work on.

grounding.model: Student Leadership Competencies — Seemiller
grounding.citation: Seemiller, The Student Leadership Competencies Guidebook; Seemiller & Rosch, Journal of Leadership Education, on the Inventory’s validation; youth competency-based model in JOLE 17(1), 2018. Inventory at studentleadershipcompetencies.com.
grounding.caveat: MBTI, DISC, learning-styles inventories and CliftonStrengths are not used in this Hub. The first three are grade C; the last is paid.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Content Research Map §1.1. Replaces the EQ Self-Assessment and Competency Self-Assessment Tracker from members.html (salvage audit: REWRITE).

cards.title: Find Your Event
cards.why: The most common reason a member drifts away after SLC is that they were assigned an event rather than fitted to one. A free federal interest inventory plus a short crosswalk routes a member to the competitive event categories that match how they actually like to work — before anyone signs them up for anything.

parts.heading: Take the profiler
parts.body: The O*NET Interest Profiler, from the U.S. Department of Labor. No account, no cost, results on screen. It scores six interest types.

parts.heading: The crosswalk
parts.body: Take your top two types and read across.
items: Investigative → Health Science events and the Academic Testing Center. You like finding out.
Social → Health Professions and the Leadership category. You like people and helping.
Realistic → Emergency Preparedness and the skills-based events. You like doing with your hands.
Enterprising → Teamwork events and the advocacy-shaped Leadership events. You like persuading and organising.
Artistic → Health Career Photography, Public Service Announcement, the presentation-heavy events.
Conventional → the Academic Testing Center, Medical Terminology, the events with a defined body of knowledge.

parts.heading: Then go to the Study Hub
parts.body: Once you have a category, the Study Hub has a tool for every event DC HOSA offers. This card gets you to the right shelf. It does not prepare you for the test — that is the Study Hub’s job, and it stays there.

steps: Take the Interest Profiler. Note your top two types.
Read across the crosswalk. List three events that fit.
Take those three to your advisor before registration closes in January.
cards.where: Before event selection every year. The crosswalk is the same one the Middle School Division uses in its careers-to-events segment — built once, used in both places.
cards.coach: Advisors assign events by what the chapter needs entered. Ask instead what the profiler said. A member in the right category competes for three years; a member in the wrong one competes once.

grounding.model: Holland RIASEC interest typology; O*NET Interest Profiler
grounding.citation: Holland’s RIASEC model; O*NET Interest Profiler, U.S. Department of Labor / Employment and Training Administration — free, validated. The event crosswalk is a DC HOSA construction.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Audience Tool Addendum M1 (build-first item).

cards.title: A Goal That Survives Contact
cards.why: Specific, hard goals beat ‘do your best’. That much is settled. But a well-formed goal is not an executed one, and the thing that closes the gap between intending and doing is naming the obstacle in advance and deciding — before it appears — exactly what you will do when it does.

parts.heading: Four lines on a card
items: Wish — one sentence. What you want to do this term.
Outcome — what it looks like when it is done. Be concrete enough to picture.
Obstacle — the internal one. Not ‘no time’; the thing in you that will get in the way. Usually a habit, a fear, or a Tuesday.
Plan — an if-then. ‘If [the obstacle shows up], then I will [specific action].’

parts.heading: Why the obstacle line is the whole card
parts.body: Positive thinking about the outcome on its own reduces the energy to pursue it. Naming the obstacle, right after picturing the outcome, is what produces the plan. The if-then is what makes the plan fire without deciding in the moment.

parts.heading: Not SMART
parts.body: SMART produces well-formed goals. This produces executed ones. If the chapter has a SMART worksheet, replace it with this.

steps: Fill the four lines for one goal this term. Wallet-size.
Read the if-then aloud. If it does not name a specific action you could do in under two minutes, rewrite it.
Check the card at the January reset.
cards.where: The start of every term. The Two-Competency plan is two of these. Healthy Living’s goal-setting is one of these with a health topic.
cards.coach: When a member’s goal fails, ask to see the obstacle line. It is nearly always missing or external. Rewrite that line with them and the goal usually works the second time.

grounding.model: Mental contrasting with implementation intentions — WOOP
grounding.citation: Oettingen, mental contrasting; Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006) meta-analysis of implementation intentions, effect around d = .65. Goal specificity per Locke & Latham (R). SMART is the practitioner packaging of the latter (P).

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Audience Tool Addendum M2. Replaces the Growth Mindset Goal Sheet from members.html (salvage audit: REWRITE).

cards.title: Reflect in Three Questions
cards.why: Reflection only happens if the structure is short enough to actually use. Three questions, three words each, and it works after a competition, after a meeting, after a week. It is the one reflection structure across this whole Hub, so that a member does not learn four competing ones.

parts.heading: The three
items: What? — what happened. Facts only. What you did, what others did, what the result was.
So what? — why it matters. What it tells you about yourself, the team, the plan.
Now what? — what you will do differently, and when.

parts.heading: Wins and losses, same three questions
parts.body: After a win, the So What is usually ‘what specifically made that work, so I can do it on purpose’. After a loss, the So What is usually ‘what was in my control’. The Now What is the same either way — one change, one date.

parts.heading: The healthcare parallel
parts.body: Every clinical role debriefs. Surgery does it after every case; emergency medicine after every shift. The habit you build here on a competition result is the one you will use on a patient outcome.

steps: After the next event, write the three answers in under five minutes.
Keep them somewhere you can find. Six of these across a year is a portfolio.
Bring the Now What to your next chapter meeting.
cards.where: After any competition, event, or leadership moment. Inside the Debrief at Team. It is what the Wins & Losses journal became.
cards.coach: Members overwrite the What with the So What — ‘I was nervous and it went badly’. Send it back once: what happened, in facts, no feelings. The reflection gets sharper immediately.

grounding.model: What? So What? Now What? — Rolfe, Freshwater & Jasper
grounding.citation: Rolfe, Freshwater & Jasper (2001), Critical Reflection for Nursing and the Helping Professions. A practitioner reflection framework; adopted here as the single structure across the Hub because it is free, three words long, and students complete it.
grounding.caveat: Kolb’s experiential learning cycle is defensible as a reflection sequence and appears in the Debrief card in that role only. The learning-styles inventory it spawned is grade C and is not used.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Content Research Map §5. Replaces the STARR-format Wins & Losses Reflection Journal from members.html (salvage audit: REWRITE, to a single reflection structure).

cards.title: Two Competencies, One Term
cards.why: A list of sixty competencies defeats itself the moment someone picks ten. Two, from different clusters, with one observable behaviour each and a named chapter activity to practise in — that is a plan an officer can actually run and a 360 can actually measure in April.

parts.heading: September
items: Take the Student Leadership Competencies Inventory if you have not. Save the result.
Choose exactly two competencies, from two different clusters. Not the two you are best at.
For each, write one behaviour someone else could observe. Not ‘be a better communicator’ — ‘open every committee report with the recommendation’.
Name the chapter activity where you will practise it. The meeting, the event, the role.

parts.heading: Through the year
parts.body: Each competency becomes a WOOP card — the obstacle line is what keeps it alive past October.

parts.heading: April
parts.body: The free 360 evaluation. Two or three people who watched you all year score the behaviour dimension. Compare to September. That is the year’s development, in a number.

steps: Pick two. Write them on the printed plan with the cluster, the behaviour, and the activity.
Turn each into a WOOP card.
Book the April 360 now, and name the people who will do it.
cards.where: Every officer, September to April. The Portfolio Charter for state officers is this plus the office’s outcome.
cards.coach: When an officer picks two competencies they are already strong in, send them back. The second choice is usually the honest one. And insist on the behaviour line — a competency without an observable behaviour cannot be scored in April, which means the year cannot be measured.

grounding.model: Student Leadership Competencies — Seemiller; goal specificity
grounding.citation: Seemiller’s competency model and the free 360 Evaluation for the behaviour dimension. Two-competency selection follows the goal-specificity finding (Locke & Latham).

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Content Research Map §1.1 (the tool to build). Replaces the Officer Self-Assessment from officers.html (salvage audit: REWRITE).

cards.title: Show Up Professionally Online
cards.why: By the time a member is an officer they have a public record whether they built it or not. DC HOSA already has a full guide to building one deliberately — a LinkedIn Professional Development Guide with a persona filter for members, officers, and advisors. This card points at it and does not rebuild it.

parts.heading: What the Guide covers
items: A profile that says what you actually do in HOSA, in terms a hospital recruiter recognises.
How to write up a competitive event, a service project, or an officer role as experience.
Who to connect with and how to ask — the informational interview is the natural first move.
What not to post, and why the standard for a future healthcare professional starts now.

parts.heading: Where it lives
parts.body: The Guide is a DC HOSA resource distributed through affiliate communications and the State Executive Council. Ask your advisor or the VP Public Relations for the current link.

steps: Open the Guide with your audience filter set.
Do the profile section this week. One hour.
Write up your most recent HOSA role in the format the Guide gives.
cards.where: Any time from Lead a Team onward. Before the first informational interview. Before applying for anything.
cards.coach: Do not let this become a lecture about social media. The Guide already exists; the officer’s job is to do the profile section. Ask to see it a week later.

grounding.model: DC HOSA LinkedIn Professional Development Guide
grounding.citation: DC HOSA LinkedIn Professional Development Guide, 2026 — the persona-filter pattern from that Guide is also the pattern this Hub uses for audience filtering.
grounding.caveat: The Guide’s canonical link is not yet recorded in hub.json. Add it to this card’s data when the hosting location is confirmed; until then the card directs members to the advisor or VP Public Relations.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Rebuild Specification §3 Self L2 — link, do not rebuild.

cards.title: Breadth Over Depth-of-One
cards.why: The only large study of what CTSO participation does found that the number of different kinds of things a member did — competition, leadership, service, professional development — was what tracked with better outcomes. A member doing one thing brilliantly is the risk profile, not the member doing several things loosely.

parts.heading: Four quadrants, three by May
items: Competition — entered an event, any event.
Leadership — held a role, ran a committee, chaired one meeting.
Community service — one project, with a real community partner.
Professional development — one informational interview, one shadowing visit, one career session.

parts.heading: What the study found, honestly
items: More types of participation went with greater academic motivation and engagement, better grades, higher career self-efficacy, and stronger college aspirations.
Of the four elements, competition showed the most positive effects.

And: the CTSO students in the study started the year ahead of the comparison group and gained less across it. This Hub does not cite the study as proof that HOSA causes achievement. It supports a breadth recommendation and nothing more.

parts.heading: Why it matters for the chapter
parts.body: A chapter that only competes loses the members who did not place. A chapter with all four quadrants gives every member a place to be good at something.

steps: Mark which quadrants you have touched this year on the printed tracker.
Pick the emptiest one. Do one thing in it before the next meeting.
Officers: count how many members have at least three by March.
cards.where: Every member, checked at the January reset. It is also the shape of the Internal Advocacy Pack an advisor takes to an administrator.
cards.coach: This is the evidence advisors reach for when a chapter is threatened by a schedule change or a budget cut, and it survives scrutiny precisely because it is not inflated. Use the honest version. Administrators have seen the other kind.

grounding.model: CTSO participation breadth — Alfeld et al.
grounding.citation: Alfeld et al. (2007), Looking Inside the Black Box: The Value Added by Career and Technical Student Organizations to Students’ High School Experience, National Research Center for Career and Technical Education.
grounding.caveat: Supports a breadth recommendation. Does not support a causal claim about achievement — the CTSO group started higher and gained less. Do not cite it as proof HOSA works.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Audience Tool Addendum M3.

cards.title: The Fifteen-Minute Interview
cards.why: A member with no clinical access has one move that costs nothing and works every time: fifteen minutes with someone who does the job, asking six questions. It produces a contact, a story for the next application, and a piece of the professional-development quadrant — and it is the first time most members find out that people say yes.

parts.heading: The ask
parts.body: Two sentences by email or through the Guide. Who you are, what you are curious about, fifteen minutes at their convenience. Nothing about a job.

parts.heading: Six questions
items: What does an ordinary day actually look like?
What did you not expect about this work?
What would you tell a student who is choosing between this and something adjacent?
What is the training path, really, and where do people get stuck?
Who else should I talk to?
Is there anything I could read or watch that would help me understand this better?

parts.heading: Within 24 hours
parts.body: A thank-you, three sentences, naming one thing they said that changed how you see the field. That note is what makes the second conversation possible.

steps: Find one person. A parent in the chapter, a partner from the ward map, someone from the advisor’s network.
Send the two-sentence ask.
Do the fifteen minutes. Send the thank-you the same day.
cards.where: The professional-development quadrant of Breadth. Before any application. The parent network — the densest professional network most chapters have and never survey — is the first place to look.
cards.coach: Members freeze on the ask, not the interview. Have them send the email during a chapter meeting, with an officer beside them. Then it is done.

grounding.model: Career self-efficacy — Bandura-derived, measured in Alfeld et al.
grounding.citation: Career self-efficacy as an outcome measure in Alfeld et al. (2007); Bandura’s self-efficacy construct. The six-question protocol is a DC HOSA construction.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Audience Tool Addendum M5 and the parent-network finding in DC-FACTS.md §11.

cards.title: Demands and Resources
cards.why: Burnout is what happens when what a role demands exceeds what it gives you to meet those demands. Engagement comes from the resources side on its own. That is a diagnosis with a lever attached: the question is not ‘are you burning out’ but ‘which single resource, if added, would change the ratio most’ — and the answer is an ask you can make.

parts.heading: Two columns
parts.body: Private. Not for submission.
items: Demands of this role, this year. Hours, deadlines, the emotional load, the things nobody else will do if you do not.
Resources available. Time, money, people, authority, recognition, a co-advisor, a student who can run a meeting, a released period.

parts.heading: Then one question
parts.body: Which single resource, if added, would change the ratio most? Not three. One. The answer becomes the ask — to a department chair, to the SEC, to the State Advisor — and the Internal Advocacy Pack is how you make it.

parts.heading: The six warning dimensions
parts.body: If you want to name where the strain is, there are six: workload, control, reward, community, fairness, values. Naming the dimension is the first step. It is not the fix — the fix is the resource.

steps: Fill both columns honestly. Ten minutes.
Circle the one resource.
Write the ask in one sentence and decide who receives it.
cards.where: Advisors in November, when the year’s shape is clear. State officers at the January reset. Anyone who has said ‘I can’t keep doing this’ out loud.
cards.coach: Advisors will fill the demands column and leave the resources column half empty because they have stopped believing there are any. Sit with them and fill it. The released period, the co-advisor, the stipend — those exist in other schools and can be asked for in this one.

grounding.model: Job Demands–Resources model — Bakker & Demerouti; Maslach burnout dimensions
grounding.citation: Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Journal of Managerial Psychology — the JD-R model. The six dimensions (workload, control, reward, community, fairness, values) after Maslach & Leiter (2001), Annual Review of Psychology.

cards.provenance: Ported and extended 12 Sep 2026 from the Advisor Sustainability Check in advisors.html (Maslach) with the JD-R extension from Audience Tool Addendum A2.

cards.title: Hand It On
cards.why: A chapter that loses its institutional memory every May restarts every September. One document, completed by each outgoing officer in an hour, is the difference between a chapter that improves and one that oscillates. The same format works for state officers and for state staff, because the problem is identical at every level.

parts.heading: The packet, one page per role
items: Passwords and where they live. Which accounts, who holds the recovery email.
Vendor, partner and contact list — the ward map, the school contacts, the people who said yes.
What we tried that worked, and why.
What we tried that failed, and why. This section is the valuable one.
The three things I would do differently.
The calendar, with the real dates attached, and which ones were derived from what.

parts.heading: Shadow before you leave
parts.body: Wherever possible the incoming officer sits beside the outgoing one for the last month — in meetings, watching decisions, asking in real time. Reconstructing context after the fact is what the packet is for; it is never as good as having been there.

parts.heading: State staff: the continuity file
parts.body: The same format applied to the roles that persist — vendor relationships, OSSE contacts, form IDs, repositories, credentials, what is on autopilot and what is not. It is the affiliate’s largest continuity risk, and the one nobody writes down because the people holding it have not left yet.

steps: Fill the packet for your role in May, before the last meeting, not after.
Walk the incoming officer through it in person. One hour.
File it where the next-but-one officer will find it.
cards.where: May, every role, every level. The midpoint memo at the January reset is the first draft.
cards.coach: The packet gets skipped because May is busy and the outgoing officer has already left in their head. Make it the last required act of the role — the certificate is handed over when the packet is. That is not harsh; it is the only thing that makes the packet exist.

grounding.model: Succession and knowledge transfer
grounding.citation: Organisational memory and volunteer succession literature; the specific packet format is a practitioner convention. Shadowing as knowledge transfer is well-documented in the nonprofit succession literature.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, collapsing the End-of-Year Advisor Reflection (advisors.html), the Annual Institutional Knowledge Handoff (state-staff.html), and Audience Tool Addendum O3 and T5 into one continuity format with audience overlays.

cards.title: The Speaking Ladder
cards.why: Nobody gets better at speaking by speaking more. They get better by speaking against one specific criterion, with immediate feedback, and then doing it again. Four rungs, one per chapter meeting, each scored on exactly one thing. One criterion is what makes it practice rather than repetition.

parts.heading: Four rungs
parts.body: Self-recorded on a phone. Scored against the one criterion only.
items: Rung 1 — a chapter announcement. Thirty seconds. Criterion: no filler words in the first sentence.
Rung 2 — a committee report. Two minutes. Criterion: opens with the recommendation, not the history.
Rung 3 — a topic presentation. Five minutes. Criterion: one idea per slide, eye contact across three zones of the room.
Rung 4 — a judged mock in the event format. Criterion: scored on the relevant competitive event rating sheet.

parts.heading: Why one criterion
parts.body: Deliberate practice is targeted repetition against a specific standard with feedback, not general effort. A member told ‘be more confident’ has nothing to practise. A member told ‘no filler in the first sentence’ can hear on the recording whether they did it.

parts.heading: Where the rungs live
parts.body: Rungs 1 and 2 are real business at real chapter meetings — the Five Moves and the committee report are already on the agenda. Rung 3 is a Health Literacy Ambassador Level 1 presentation. Rung 4 is the mock before SLC.

steps: Do rung 1 at the next meeting. Record it. Listen for the first sentence only.
Do not move to rung 2 until rung 1 is clean twice.
Officers: put a rung on every meeting agenda, rotating who climbs.
cards.where: Every chapter meeting. You will already be ready for Prepared Speaking and Speaking Skills, and for the presentation round of any event that has one.
cards.coach: Resist giving more than one note. If the member’s first sentence was clean, say so and stop, even if the rest was rough. Next rung, next criterion. The whole method depends on the note count being one.

grounding.model: Deliberate practice — Ericsson
grounding.citation: Ericsson, Krampe & Tesch-Römer (1993), Psychological Review — deliberate practice as targeted repetition against a specific criterion with immediate feedback.

cards.provenance: New card, 12 Sep 2026, from Content Research Map §4.1 (the tool to build). Absorbs the ‘thirty-second announcement’ and ‘committee report’ topics from the spec’s Voice map as rungs 1 and 2.

cards.title: Nerves Are Fuel
cards.why: Telling yourself to calm down before you speak does not work, because calm and nervous are far apart and the body does not travel that distance in sixty seconds. Nervous and excited are almost the same state. Saying ‘I am excited’ out loud, once, outperformed trying to calm down — across speaking, singing, and maths tasks.

parts.heading: The one sentence
parts.body: Out loud, before you walk in: ‘I am excited.’ Not ‘I am calm.’ Not ‘I am fine.’ The point is not to believe it. The point is that it reframes the racing heart as readiness rather than threat, and that changes what you do next.

parts.heading: What it replaces
items: Deep breathing to reach calm — works slowly, and you do not have slowly.
‘Picture the audience in their underwear’ and the rest of the folklore.

The old build’s speaker model, which listed preparation, past success, self-esteem and support as the sources of confidence. All true, none of them available in the sixty seconds before a competitive event room. This is.

parts.heading: Then the exposure
parts.body: Reappraisal is for the moment. Graduated exposure is for the year — the Speaking Ladder is the exposure schedule.

steps: Say it before the next thing you present. Out loud. Once.
Notice what your body does with the same heart rate under the new label.
Keep climbing the ladder — the reappraisal works better each time it is paired with a rung.
cards.where: The corridor outside any competitive event room. Before any presentation. Before testifying.
cards.coach: Do not teach relaxation techniques for the sixty-second window. Teach this sentence, and reserve breathing and preparation for the weeks before. The member who says ‘I am excited’ walks in differently, and you can see it.

grounding.model: Anxiety reappraisal — Brooks
grounding.citation: Brooks (2014), Journal of Experimental Psychology: General — reappraising pre-performance anxiety as excitement outperformed attempts to calm down. Graduated exposure for public-speaking anxiety has meta-analytic support.

cards.title: One Idea Per Slide
cards.why: ‘Your slides have too much text’ sounds like taste. It is not — it is a claim about how much a listener can process at once, and there is a mechanism behind it. Five principles, one line each, applied by the presenter before anyone else sees the deck.

parts.heading: The five-line check
items: Coherence — cut anything that does not serve the point. The decorative image, the third bullet, the logo on every slide.
Signalling — cue what matters. Bold the one number. Put the recommendation at the top.
Redundancy — do not read on-screen text aloud. If it is on the slide, say something else.
Modality — narrate the graphic; do not caption it. Words in the air plus a picture on the screen beats words on the screen plus the same words in the air.
Segmenting — one idea per slide, and let the listener control the pace where you can.

parts.heading: Why this version lands with students
parts.body: Because it is a cognitive-load claim, not a design opinion. The listener has one channel for words and one for pictures; overload either and nothing gets through. That is a mechanism a health science student accepts.

parts.heading: The competitive-event variant
parts.body: Each principle maps to a criterion on the presentation rating sheets — organisation, visual aids, delivery. Practice for the chapter and preparation for the event are the same activity.

steps: Run the five lines on your last deck. Score each one yes or no.
Fix the worst one. Usually redundancy.
Rung 3 of the Speaking Ladder is scored on this.
cards.where: Every presentation. Health Education, Public Service Announcement, Community Awareness, the Ambassador Level 1 presentation — all of them.
cards.coach: When a member defends a crowded slide, ask which of the five principles it passes. The argument ends there, because it is no longer about preference.

grounding.model: Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning — Mayer
grounding.citation: Mayer, Multimedia Learning (2nd ed., 2009) — coherence, signalling, redundancy, modality and segmenting principles; one of the most replicated bodies of instructional-design research.

cards.title: The Committee Report
cards.why: Most committee reports tell the meeting what the committee did. The meeting does not need to know that. It needs to know what the committee recommends, so it can decide. Open with the recommendation; the history is available if anyone asks.

parts.heading: The structure
parts.body: Two minutes, in this order.
items: The recommendation. ‘The fundraising committee recommends a bake sale on 14 February, run by the sophomores, target three hundred dollars.’
The one reason. ‘The fun run needs a permit we cannot get in time.’
The decision needed. ‘We need a vote to adopt, and a volunteer to book the cafeteria.’
Then stop. Questions will surface anything else.

parts.heading: Report versus recommendation
parts.body: A report informs — here is what happened. A recommendation asks the body to act. The chair needs to know which one is coming, because only the second one gets a motion. Say which it is in the first five words.

parts.heading: If you must tell a story
parts.body: One shape, when the meeting needs to understand a situation before it can decide: the situation as it was, the complication that changed it, the question that raises, and your answer. Four sentences. It is the only narrative structure this Hub teaches, because one is enough.

steps: Rewrite your next report with the recommendation as the first sentence.
Cut everything that happened before the recommendation was reached.
Rung 2 of the Speaking Ladder. Record it; check the first sentence.
cards.where: February of One Motion a Month, where committee reports are the month’s procedure. Every SEC meeting.
cards.coach: When a report runs long, the fix is never ‘be briefer’. It is ‘what are you asking us to decide’. Ask that, and the two minutes appear.

grounding.model: Recommendation-first reporting; SCQA structure
grounding.citation: RONR 12th ed. §51 on committee reports and recommendations (R). The situation–complication–question–answer structure is a practitioner framework (Minto), retained as the single narrative structure and labelled accordingly.

cards.title: Write So People Act
cards.why: A chapter email that nobody acts on was not read badly; it was written so that no action was findable. Plain language is a federal standard with a short rulebook, and applying it to a chapter announcement takes five minutes and roughly halves the length.

parts.heading: The rules that do the most work
items: The action first. What do you want them to do, by when. First line, not last.
One topic per message. Two topics is two messages.
Short sentences, common words, active voice. ‘Bring your form on Tuesday’, not ‘forms should be submitted by attendees prior to the Tuesday session’.
Headings and lists for anything longer than a paragraph. Nobody reads a wall.
The reader’s question, answered — ‘what does this mean for me’ — before your reason for writing.

parts.heading: For health material, score it
parts.body: Anything that is patient education — a flyer, a handout, a poster — gets the PEMAT score from Community as well. Plain language is the writing; PEMAT is the check.

parts.heading: For the affiliate
parts.body: State staff and the SEC can adopt the federal plain-language guidance as a house standard in one meeting. A Chartered Association that asks chapters to communicate clearly should be able to show it does.

steps: Take the last chapter message you sent. Put the action in the first line.
Cut it by half.
Send the shorter one next time and count the replies.
cards.where: Every chapter and affiliate communication. The newsletter column. Anything with a deadline in it.
cards.coach: Read the SEC’s last three advisor emails with the five rules in hand. Score them. If the affiliate’s own writing fails, that is the first fix, before any chapter is asked to change.

grounding.model: Plain language — federal guidelines
grounding.citation: Federal Plain Language Guidelines, plainlanguage.gov (Plain Writing Act of 2010). PEMAT for patient education material per the Community domain.
grounding.caveat: Re-verify the plainlanguage.gov link before adopting formally.

cards.title: Make an Ask
cards.why: Youth advocacy fails in a specific way: plenty of voice, no audience. Members write, post, present — and nobody with the power to act was in the room. A four-box checklist tells you whether a campaign is real before you run it, and a 16-year-old can audit their own in ten minutes.

parts.heading: Four boxes — all four, or it is not participation
items: Space — is there a safe, inclusive place for the members to form and express a view?
Voice — are they supported to say it? Information, time, the words.
Audience — is someone with the power to act actually listening? Named. In the room, or receiving the document.
Influence — will the view be acted on, and will the members be told what happened and why?

parts.heading: The box DC students miss
parts.body: Audience. A campaign with Space and Voice and no Audience is an assembly. DC has something most affiliates lack: a city council whose committees accept public testimony, including from young people. That is an Audience with a calendar.

parts.heading: Then the One-Page Ask
parts.body: See Testify. The ask is what you put in front of the Audience once you have found one.

steps: Audit your current campaign against the four boxes. Write yes or no on each.
If Audience is no, stop. Find one — the ward map has candidates; the Council calendar has hearings.
If Influence is no, decide how members will hear back. That is part of the design, not an afterthought.
cards.where: Any advocacy the chapter or SEC runs. Researched Persuasive Writing & Speaking and Extemporaneous Writing – Health Policy are this, in competition form.
cards.coach: When an officer proposes an awareness campaign, ask who the Audience is by name. If the answer is ‘the community’ or ‘students’, there is no Audience yet, and the campaign is not ready.

grounding.model: Lundy Model of Participation — Space, Voice, Audience, Influence
grounding.citation: Lundy (2007), British Educational Research Journal — a rights-based model with published implementation evidence; used as the design spine of youth advocacy programmes including Amplify and Advocate (Journal of Community Psychology, 2025).
